title: Bounced Checks and Returned Payments
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no civil statute capping the fee a landlord may charge for a returned rent payment; a fee in the lease should be reasonable. Writing a check knowing it will not be paid is a crime. On conviction, the court orders repayment of the check, interest and a service charge of up to $50 (or the payee's actual bank fees if higher), but only if a written notice of the service charge was conspicuously displayed at the payee's premises when the check was given. After a conviction and a written demand at least 10 days before suit, the payee may sue for the greater of $100 or three times the check, limited to $500 more than the check's value.

title: Pennsylvania Landlord and Tenant Law: What Applies
bodyText: Pennsylvania's main landlord-tenant statute is The Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951, an unconsolidated act cited as 68 P.S. § 250.101 (Act § 101) and following. It is short: it covers written and oral leases, notices to quit, eviction before a magisterial district judge, security deposits, property left behind, death of a tenant, drug-related removal, and rights of tenants in buildings with three or more households. It does not set entry notice, late-fee limits, a landlord repair code or a general retaliation rule; much of Pennsylvania landlord-tenant law, including the implied warranty of habitability, comes from court decisions. A 'tenant' includes anyone occupying with the owner's express or implied consent, by oral or written lease or by the owner's acceptance of rent; the Act does not apply to a person who is not and never has been a tenant. A lease of more than three years must be in writing and signed; if it is not, it has the effect of a tenancy at will only, unless the tenancy has lasted more than one year and both sides have treated it as valid by claiming and paying the rent, in which case it becomes a year-to-year tenancy. A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's rights and duties, and a subtenant is bound by the lease. Local ordinances, especially in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, add rules this library does not cover.

title: Pennsylvania Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: A residential security deposit may not exceed two months' rent in the first year of a lease and one month's rent in the second and later years or on renewal; after five years' possession a rent increase cannot require a larger deposit. Deposits over $100 must be held in an escrow account at a regulated institution, and the landlord must tell the tenant in writing the institution's name and address and the amount; a guarantee bond may be used instead. After the second anniversary of the deposit, the account must earn interest: the landlord keeps 1% a year as its only administrative charge and pays the rest to the tenant every year on the lease anniversary. Within 30 days after the lease ends or the landlord accepts surrender, the landlord must give a written list of damage and refund the balance with unpaid interest. Missing the 30-day list forfeits all rights to withhold any part of the deposit and to sue for damage to the property; a late or short refund can cost double the amount wrongly kept. Otherwise the landlord may keep the deposit for unpaid rent or another breach; whether that survives a missed list is not settled by the statute's text. A tenant who does not give a new address in writing relieves the landlord of liability under the return section. None of these rules can be waived. Whether last month's rent paid in advance counts toward the cap is not settled by the statute. An uncashed refund may become unclaimed property reportable to the State Treasurer after three years.

title: Notice to Quit (Notice to Move Out)
bodyText: Before filing to recover possession, a Pennsylvania landlord gives the tenant a written notice to quit unless the lease waives it or shortens it. The periods are: 10 days for failure to pay rent after demand; 15 days at the end of a lease of one year or less, a lease with no fixed end, or a forfeiture for breach of such a lease; 30 days at the end of, or on forfeiture of, a lease of more than one year; and 10 days where the lease ends for illegal drug activity. Which period applies depends on the kind of tenancy, not on what the lease calls itself. By the statute's wording, a week-to-week, month-to-month or year-to-year tenancy (each term is one year or less) and a tenancy at will (no fixed end) all get 15 days; only a fixed term longer than one year gets 30 days. The 10-day notice for unpaid rent is the same for every kind of tenancy. The notice may be handed to the tenant, left at the main building on the premises, or posted conspicuously on the premises. A lease may provide a shorter notice or a waiver. Mobile-home park spaces follow different, longer rules. The notice rules do not apply to someone who is not and never was a tenant. Federal law may require a 30-day notice for properties with federally backed mortgages or federal assistance, whatever the lease says. The library's default clause doesn't promise written notice of a rent default beyond what Pennsylvania law requires. You may still give written notice of the default before filing, and that is good practice: if the lease also uses the optional notice-to-quit waiver, a tenant may otherwise get no warning at all before you file.

title: Eviction in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Eviction starts with a complaint before the magisterial district judge where the property is (in Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Municipal Court). The complaint states that notice to quit was given or that the lease required none, and for each tenant the landlord attaches an affidavit about military service. The hearing is set 7 to 15 days after filing, and the landlord must appear and prove the case even if the tenant does not come; there is no default judgment. Some counties offer or require mediation by local rule. If the landlord wins, the judgment covers possession, unpaid rent, damages for unjust detention, physical damage and costs. For a residential lease the landlord may request an order for possession after the 10th day and within 120 days after judgment; the officer serves it, and may remove the tenant on or after the 11th day after service. In a case for unpaid rent only, the tenant can stop the removal by paying the rent in arrears and costs before possession is delivered. A tenant may appeal to the court of common pleas within 10 days (30 days for a victim of domestic violence, who may also file an affidavit that holds off removal for up to 30 days after judgment). An appeal stops the eviction only if the tenant deposits the lesser of three months' rent or the rent in arrears and then pays each month's rent into court, or files a low-income affidavit. Where the appeal goes to compulsory arbitration and the arbitrators rule for the tenant, the court rules' official commentary says the landlord may not obtain an order for possession between the entry of that award and the landlord's own appeal, even if the tenant stops paying into court. A judgment for possession by confession is not available on a residential lease signed by an individual. Wages may be attached for up to 10% of net pay on a final residential-lease judgment, but not against a protected abuse victim for physical damage the abuser caused. Only a court officer may remove a tenant.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: Pennsylvania's eviction procedure is the only lawful way to remove a tenant: only a constable or sheriff executing an order for possession may enter by force and put a tenant out. The 1951 Act describes itself as a complete and exclusive system. No Pennsylvania statute sets a specific money penalty for a lockout, but courts treat self-help as unlawful, and a landlord who disposes of or takes control of property in an occupied unit without the tenant's express permission owes treble damages, attorney fees and costs. A landlord who holds the utility account may not have service shut off at its request unless the tenants agree, and may not retaliate against tenants who pay the utility to keep service on.

title: Retaliation Protections
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general anti-retaliation statute for residential tenants, but several statutes protect specific acts. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a lease because a tenant or family member takes part in a tenants' organization. A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals against a tenant for paying a landlord's unpaid utility bill to keep service on, or for deducting that payment from rent, owes the greater of two months' rent or actual damages, plus costs and attorney fees, and a notice to end the tenancy, a rent increase or a substantial change in terms within six months is presumed retaliatory. In cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, a tenant may not be evicted for any reason while rent is paid into escrow for a unit certified unfit. A municipality may not, by ordinance, penalize a resident, tenant or landlord for calls for police or emergency help by or for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, if the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it actually was.

title: Rent Withholding for Units Certified Unfit
bodyText: In a city of the first, second, second class A or third class, if the city's code or health agency, or the county health department, certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation, the tenant's duty to pay rent and the landlord's right to collect it are suspended until the unit is certified fit or the tenancy ends for a reason other than nonpayment. A tenant who stays pays the rent into an approved escrow account. The escrow goes to the landlord if the unit is certified fit within six months of the unfit certification; otherwise it goes back to the tenant, except that it may be used to make repairs and to pay utilities the landlord is obliged to pay. No tenant may be evicted for any reason while rent is in escrow. The certifying agency must send the landlord a monthly statement of the escrowed funds.

title: Habitability and Repairs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lists a residential landlord's repair duties. Pennsylvania courts recognize an implied warranty of habitability in residential leases, which a lease cannot waive, and local housing and property-maintenance codes set the working standards. By statute, a landlord of a building or complex with three or more households must use reasonable care to keep stairways, passages, roadways and other common facilities safe for tenants and their guests, and tenants must obey applicable codes and must not damage the property or disturb other tenants. In certain cities a unit certified unfit triggers rent withholding. Courts may set up housing courts for code and landlord-tenant cases. Under the state blight law, an owner who takes no substantial step within six months of an order to correct a serious code violation can be sued personally by the municipality, have other assets liened and be denied municipal permits for other properties; repeat convictions for the same serious violation are a crime; and an out-of-state owner charged with a code crime may be extradited.

title: When the Landlord Holds the Utility Account
bodyText: If a landlord is the utility's customer for gas, electric, steam, water or sewer serving tenants, the utility must give the landlord 37 days' written notice before shutting service off for nonpayment and must notify the tenants at least 30 days ahead. The landlord must give the utility the tenants' names and addresses within 7 days of a request unless it pays or arranges to pay; failing to do so costs $500 to $1,000 a day in liquidated damages. Tenants may pay the bill for the last month to keep service on, then deduct what they paid from rent or recover it from the landlord. A landlord may not retaliate against them. A landlord who asks the utility to end service must certify that the units are vacant or the tenants consent, have the tenants tell the utility they consent, or give the utility the tenants' names so it can notify them. Owners of rental buildings with units that are not individually metered must tell each utility that the property is rented, and they remain responsible for the bills. A utility two or more months unpaid may ask the court to appoint a receiver to collect rents. Tenants cannot waive these rights. Separately, where a municipal authority or a third class city supplies water or sewer service through a tenant's own account at a unit the owner does not live in, the owner can be made to pay the tenant's unpaid bill if the authority or city notifies both the owner and the tenant within 30 days after the bill first becomes overdue; for water, the owner is not liable for service more than 90 days after it became overdue unless a court order stopped the shutoff.

title: Plain Language Rules for Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Plain Language Consumer Contract Act applies to residential leases (not commercial leases or contracts over $50,000). A lease must be written, organized and designed to be easy to read. Courts consider whether it uses short words, sentences and paragraphs; active verbs; few legal terms; no Latin; personal pronouns or the parties' names; one condition per sentence; clear cross references; no double negatives; readable type size, line length, margins and spacing; boldface section captions; and sharply contrasting ink. It must also carry a statement describing what the tenant could lose on default and listing the tenant's waivers of rights. A landlord that fails the test owes the tenant actual loss, $100, costs and attorney fees, unless it made a good-faith and reasonable effort to comply; the lease stays valid and class actions are barred. The Attorney General will preapprove a lease on request; its guideline is an average of 25 words or fewer per sentence and 60 per paragraph. The Act excludes consumer contracts involving more than $50,000, and the text does not say how that amount is measured for a lease (for example, total rent over the term), so a high-rent or long lease may fall outside it.

title: Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Many older Pennsylvania leases let the landlord 'confess judgment' against the tenant without a hearing. A confessed judgment for possession is abolished for a residential lease signed by an individual, so a landlord must use the ordinary eviction process. Confession of judgment for money is abolished for consumer credit transactions; whether that reaches a residential lease is not settled by the rule's text, and courts view these clauses with suspicion. The library includes no confession-of-judgment clause for Pennsylvania.

title: Electronic Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Electronic Transactions Act gives electronic records and signatures legal effect when the parties agree to act electronically. But a paper consumer contract, such as a lease signed on paper, may authorize doing business electronically only if the tenant agrees in a separate and express acknowledgment that says which parts of the transaction will be electronic and how. Using e-payment alone does not show agreement. Federal law separately says electronic delivery cannot replace paper for notices of default or eviction on a primary residence. Pennsylvania's notice-to-quit statute lists its own delivery methods: personal delivery, leaving it at the main building, or conspicuous posting.

title: Pennsylvania Fair Housing Law
bodyText: The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act bars housing discrimination because of race (including hair texture and protective hairstyles), color, familial status, age (40 and over), religious creed, ancestry, sex, national origin, handicap or disability, a known relationship with a person with a disability, or use of a guide or support animal. It adds age to the federal classes. A landlord may not evict before the end of the lease because of pregnancy or the birth of a child, and may not ask questions, keep records or use application forms about protected characteristics. Landlords must allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (with restoration where reasonable) and make reasonable accommodations. Every covered landlord must post the Human Relations Commission's fair practices notice in its place of business. The Act does not cover renting part of an owner-occupied building of no more than two units, a room in a landlord-occupied rooming house with a common entrance, or qualifying housing for older persons. Occupancy limits based on bedrooms and unit size are allowed. Pennsylvania has no statewide source-of-income protection.

title: Pennsylvania Service and Assistance Animal Law
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act lets a landlord ask for documentation of a disability and the need for an assistance or service animal only when the disability or need is not readily apparent or known to the landlord. The documentation must be written, reliable, based on direct knowledge of the person's disability and need, and must describe the need. An 'assistance animal' includes an emotional support animal that qualifies as a reasonable accommodation. A landlord is not liable for injuries caused by an assistance or service animal it permits as a reasonable accommodation. Lying about a disability or need, or making materially false statements to obtain documentation, to get an animal accepted in housing is a third-degree misdemeanor; creating false papers or putting a service vest on an animal that is not one is a summary offense with a fine up to $1,000. The Human Relations Act separately bars refusing to rent because a person uses a guide or support animal. Pennsylvania's criminal service-dog discrimination statute covers places of public accommodation, not rental housing.

title: Servicemember Rights in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Besides the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, Pennsylvania lets a member of the U.S. armed forces, or of the Pennsylvania National Guard on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, end a housing lease on at least 30 days' written notice after receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than three months, an honorable discharge or release, or orders to government quarters that forfeit the housing allowance. The tenant must give the landlord a copy of the orders, or a commanding officer's letter, before the termination date. Final rent is prorated; rent paid in advance for after the termination must be refunded within 30 days; a court may modify the relief if the landlord applies before the termination date. Holding a servicemember's deposit or belongings to force payment of rent after a lawful termination is a summary offense. For Guard and reserve members called to active duty, no eviction may be made without leave of court, and the court may stay the case for six months.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: If the only tenant on a residential lease dies during the term, the executor or administrator of the estate may end the lease by giving the landlord 14 days' written notice, effective on the later of the last day of the second calendar month after the month of death or the date the unit is surrendered and all the tenant's property removed. The estate still owes rent and other debts up to the termination, including damage to the premises and costs the landlord incurs because of the death, but owes no penalty or damages for ending early. The rule applies to leases entered into or extended after it took effect in 2016. Property a deceased tenant leaves behind is handled under Pennsylvania estate law, not the abandoned-property rules.

title: Drug and Other Criminal Activity at the Property
bodyText: By statute, a first conviction for selling, making or distributing illegal drugs on the rented dwelling or any part of a multiple dwelling, a second violation of the drug laws there, or a police seizure of illegal drugs on the leased premises, is a breach of the lease and grounds to remove the tenant, on a 10-day notice to quit. Not acting on one violation does not waive the landlord's rights for later ones. Separately, the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act lets a landlord, a tenant organization, a district attorney or, at a district attorney's request, the Attorney General bring an expedited civil action in the court of common pleas to evict tenants or remove other people involved in drug-related criminal activity on or near leased residential premises. Neighbors, tenants and others may also sue under the Drug Nuisance Law, where a court can order repairs, security measures, rent escrow for up to 90 days, a rent trustee or suspension of subsidies until the nuisance ends. For a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program, federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: A Pennsylvania municipality may not penalize a tenant, resident or landlord because police or emergency help was called by or for a victim of abuse or crime, or a person in an emergency, when the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it actually was. 'Penalize' includes revoking, suspending or refusing to renew a rental license, fines, and evicting or causing an eviction. A tenant or landlord may sue the municipality for an order to stop, damages, attorney fees, costs and reinstatement of a rental license. Local nuisance or disorderly-property ordinances that conflict are preempted. The rule does not limit the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act or alarm-device ordinances.

title: Tenant Rights in Buildings with Three or More Households
bodyText: In a building or complex with three or more households, a tenant may invite employees, business visitors, tradespeople, delivery people and suppliers of goods and services, and may have social guests, family and visitors for a reasonable time, as long as the tenant meets the tenant's obligations. A lease cannot waive these rights, and the landlord may not charge a fee or extra rent for them or restrict where the tenant buys goods and services. The landlord owes reasonable care for the safety of common areas it controls. Tenants may also order cable television from a franchised operator; the landlord may not charge different rent to cable subscribers and non-subscribers, and it deals with the operator over installation terms and compensation.

title: Condominium and Cooperative Conversion
bodyText: When a rented building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the developer must give each residential tenant a conversion notice at least one year before requiring the tenant to move, by hand delivery or certified or registered mail, with a public offering statement. For six months the tenant has the right to buy the unit, and for six months after that the unit may not be offered to others on better terms. During the notice year the tenant cannot be required to move out, even if the lease ends sooner, except for nonpayment of rent, waste, or conduct that disturbs other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. The lease terms cannot be changed during that year but can be enforced, and failing to give notice is a defense to eviction. After receiving the notice the tenant may end the lease on 90 days' written notice without liability. Coercion, harassment and withholding services are banned. A tenant who is 62 or older or disabled, lives in the unit as a principal residence (in a condominium or planned community, for at least two years) and proves eligibility within 60 days of the notice may stay for two years after the notice on the same limited grounds, with any rent increase in that extension capped at the lesser of 5% or the rise in the cost of living.

title: Towing from Rental Property
bodyText: Nobody may park or leave a vehicle on private property without the consent of the owner or the person in possession, except in an emergency or breakdown. The rule reaches private parking lots only if they are posted with the parking restrictions. The owner or person in possession may have a violating vehicle removed at the vehicle owner's reasonable expense and has a lien for the removal and storage costs; unless the municipality sets rates, storage is limited to $25 a day. Municipalities may regulate towing rates and towers, and Philadelphia has its own removal rules. A 2026 law adds penalties for improper towing at accident scenes and for towing storage facilities, effective December 2026; it does not govern private-lot towing.

title: Distress for Rent
bodyText: The 1951 Act still prints an old remedy called distress: seizing and selling a tenant's belongings from the premises for unpaid rent, with appraisal, notice and sale by a constable, and exemptions for $300 of property, clothing, Bibles, school books and some other items. The Rules of Civil Procedure for district judges do not cover it, its use against residential tenants has been challenged in the courts as unconstitutional, and a landlord who distrains wrongly faces damages up to double or treble. The library does not use or offer distress, and Pennsylvania landlords should not rely on it without a lawyer.

title: Selling or Losing a Rented Property
bodyText: A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's rights and duties toward the tenant. After a sheriff's or other judicial sale, the purchaser may collect rent as landlord from the date of its deed; a tenant whose lease is older than the judgment or mortgage behind the sale keeps a right to possession that outranks the purchaser, and rent paid in advance is protected unless paid with notice of the proceedings or to defeat the purchaser. A tenant for years has no priority over a tax-sale purchaser. After a foreclosure, federal law generally requires 90 days' notice to bona fide tenants. Utilities may ask a court to appoint a receiver to collect rents when a landlord falls two months behind on master-metered service.

title: Lead-Based Paint
bodyText: Federal law requires the lead warning statement, disclosure of known lead hazards, available records and the EPA pamphlet before renting pre-1978 housing. Pennsylvania adds no statewide landlord disclosure, testing or abatement duty for rentals; its Lead Certification Act licenses lead inspectors and abatement contractors. Philadelphia requires lead-safe or lead-free certification for many rentals, and other cities have their own rules.

title: Carbon Monoxide and Smoke Alarms
bodyText: Owners of rental apartment buildings with three or more households must install an approved carbon monoxide alarm in each apartment that has a fossil fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, replace missing alarms before a new tenant moves in and make sure the batteries work at move-in; tenants maintain, test and replace batteries during the tenancy and report problems in writing. Willful failure is a summary offense with a fine up to $50. One- and two-family homes have only a disclosure duty when sold. Pennsylvania has no statute requiring landlords to provide smoke alarms in rentals; building codes and local ordinances may, and municipalities may set stricter carbon monoxide rules.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Pennsylvania does not cap residential late fees or require a grace period. A fee that is out of proportion to the landlord's actual loss may be refused by a court as a penalty.

title: No Statutory Entry Notice
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets how much notice a landlord must give before entering a rental unit, or when it may enter. The lease controls, subject to local ordinances and the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment. The library's Access & Entry clause requires at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency.

title: No Rent Increase Notice Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute on how much notice a landlord must give before raising rent or how much it may raise it; there is no statewide rent control. The narrow exception is a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, where the tenant's terms may not be altered during the year after the conversion notice and an eligible tenant 62 or older or disabled who stays on longer may face an increase of no more than the lesser of 5% or the statutory price-index change. During a fixed-term lease the rent is what the lease says. For a month-to-month tenancy, a change is usually made by ending the tenancy with the required notice and offering new terms. Raising rent in retaliation for protected utility payments is presumed unlawful for six months.

title: No Application Fee Limit
bodyText: Pennsylvania sets no dollar cap on rental application fees. From December 21, 2026, a landlord or its agent may charge only a fee reasonably related to the actual administrative expenses incurred, and may not use application fees as a general source of revenue. The law neither requires nor bans an application fee. Fair housing law still bars application questions about protected characteristics.

title: No Domestic Violence Lease Termination Right
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute letting a domestic violence victim end a private residential lease early, change the locks or remove an abuser from the lease. Protections that do exist: a victim of domestic violence gets 30 days, instead of 10, to appeal an eviction judgment; a landlord who knows of a protection-from-abuse order must hold the tenant's belongings 30 days after an eviction; wages cannot be attached against a protected victim for physical damage the abuser caused; municipalities may not penalize calls for help; public housing authority tenants may request emergency relocation; and a protection-from-abuse order can give the victim possession of a home the parties lease together and exclude the abuser (the statute does not address the lease itself).

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute sealing or limiting public access to eviction case records. Court access policies may limit some information.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Pennsylvania requires no radon testing or disclosure for rentals. Radon appears in the seller disclosure rules for home sales and in radon-tester certification laws, not in landlord-tenant law.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring landlords to disclose bed bugs or setting treatment timelines. The implied warranty of habitability and local codes still apply.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring landlords to disclose mold or setting treatment timelines. The implied warranty of habitability and local codes still apply.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Pennsylvania requires no flood-zone or flood-history disclosure to tenants.

title: No Drug Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring landlords to disclose a former methamphetamine or other drug lab, or to decontaminate before renting. A person convicted of running a clandestine lab can be ordered to pay cleanup costs.

title: No Statewide Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Pennsylvania law does not require landlords to accept housing choice vouchers or bar discrimination based on lawful source of income. Some cities, including Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, do; those ordinances are outside this library.

title: No Rent Receipt Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give receipts for cash rent. A landlord should still keep a written record of every payment.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Pennsylvania gives tenants no statutory right to install an electric vehicle charger.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania does not require a move-in inspection or inventory. Because the landlord must prove damage to keep any of the deposit, a signed move-in condition report is strongly recommended.

title: No Owner or Manager Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania law does not require a residential lease to name the owner or an agent for notices. Owners of rental buildings with shared utility meters must notify the utility that the property is rented. Philadelphia and other cities require rental licenses that identify owners.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: Pennsylvania caps residential security deposits by statute. The cap applies whether or not the lease mentions it, and a tenant cannot waive it. During the first year of a lease, a landlord may not require more than two months' rent as a deposit. In the second and later years, and on any renewal, the amount required may not exceed one month's rent. Once a tenant has been in possession for five years, a rent increase cannot require a larger deposit. Money held against damage or unpaid rent counts toward the cap, including a pet deposit. The statute does not say what happens to a first-year deposit of more than one month's rent when the second year begins; the cautious course is to return the excess then and to require no more than one month's rent on renewal. Whether last month's rent paid in advance counts toward the cap is not settled by the statute. The statute counts by years of a lease and by renewals and does not say how that works for a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, where each new period could be read as a renewal of the original lease. A landlord who wants to avoid the question can hold no more than one month's rent for a periodic tenancy, or have a Pennsylvania lawyer confirm that the two-month first-year limit applies.

title: Setting Your Own Lease Terms for Property Left Behind
bodyText: Pennsylvania's abandoned-property statute sets a default procedure: a written notice by first class mail, 10 days from the postmark for the tenant to collect the property or ask for storage, and storage for up to 30 days, at the tenant's cost, if asked. The statute also says that where a written lease conflicts with it, the lease controls. So a landlord may write its own terms for property left behind into the lease, for example a shorter collection period or no storage. The limits: (1) The protection-from-abuse hold cannot be changed: after an order for possession is carried out, a landlord who knows of a protection-from-abuse order protecting the tenant or a member of the tenant's immediate family may not dispose of or take control of the property for 30 days from the notice, and must store it for up to 30 days if asked. (2) The statute says that under no circumstances may a landlord dispose of or take control of property in a unit someone still lives in without the tenant's express permission; whether a lease term could change that is not settled, so a lease term should not try. (3) Only a written lease can change the procedure. (4) A term that takes away the tenant's statutory rights is a waiver the lease's statement of consumer restrictions must list, and it must be written in plain language. (5) The statute does not reach a deceased tenant's property, which goes through estate law, and manufactured-home communities have their own rules. (6) A landlord that violates the statute owes triple damages, attorney fees and court costs, so have a Pennsylvania lawyer review any custom term. This library's lease clause follows the statute.

title: No General Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania state law has no general just-cause or good-cause rule for residential tenancies: when a lease term ends and the landlord gives the required notice to quit, the landlord does not need a reason. A few statutes limit this in specific situations. A landlord may not end or refuse to renew a lease because the tenant or a family member takes part in a tenants' organization. In cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, a tenant may not be evicted for any reason while rent is paid into escrow for a unit certified unfit. When a building is converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, tenants cannot be required to move out during the notice year except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing conduct. Manufactured-home community lots have their own good-cause rules, and some cities, including Philadelphia, have local good-cause rules this library does not cover.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no state statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on sharing rent data between landlords. Federal and state antitrust and consumer-protection law still apply.

title: No Statute Treating Fees as Rent
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether late fees, utility charges or other fees count as rent, so it depends on the lease. Many Pennsylvania leases call such charges 'additional rent'; whether an eviction for nonpayment can rest on unpaid fees is a question for the courts. One limit is written into the statute: in a building with three or more households, a landlord may not charge any fee, service charge or additional rent for the tenant's right to have guests, workers, delivery people and suppliers. This library's clauses do not label fees as rent.

title: No Statutory Landlord Right to Cure a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute letting a landlord fix a tenant's breach, such as damage or a maintenance failure, and bill the cost to the tenant as rent. The lease may give that right, and a landlord may otherwise recover the cost as damages or from the security deposit.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach. Complete every blank before signing anyway: a blank leaves the term unclear, and Pennsylvania's plain-language law for consumer contracts, which covers residential leases, requires the lease to be clear and understandable.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute states a landlord's covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment for residential leases. Pennsylvania court decisions, rather than a statute, treat leases as carrying an implied promise of quiet enjoyment, so a landlord who substantially interferes with the tenant's use of the home can be liable even if the lease says nothing.

title: Forms Pennsylvania Law Supplies
bodyText: Pennsylvania's landlord-tenant statute supplies one form: the notice to a tenant about property left behind, which must be sent by first class mail to the rental address and to any forwarding or emergency address the tenant gave, in substantially this form: "Personal property remaining at (address) is now considered to have been abandoned. Within ten days of the postmark date of this notice, you must retrieve any items you wish to keep or contact your landlord at (telephone number and address) to request that the property be retained or stored. If requested, storage will be provided for up to thirty days from the postmark date of this notice at a place of your landlord's choosing, and you will be responsible for costs of storage." Note that the form counts storage from the postmark date, while the statute's own rule counts the 30 days from the date of the notice; dating and mailing the notice the same day avoids the gap. Eviction filings before a magisterial district judge use court forms prescribed by the courts. Pennsylvania does not supply a statutory lease form or notice-to-quit form.

title: No Rule on Tenant Security Cameras or Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute addresses whether a tenant may install security cameras or video doorbells; the lease controls, including its rules on alterations. A device that records sound is different: Pennsylvania's wiretap law generally makes it a crime to record a conversation without consent where the speakers expect privacy, so a camera or doorbell that captures audio in shared hallways or neighbors' spaces can raise that issue.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If a Pennsylvania tenant, someone in the household or a guest damages the home, the statutes give you a few tools. You may keep the security deposit for the actual damage the tenant caused, but only if you give the tenant a written list of the damage within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept the tenant's surrender, whichever comes first; missing the list forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit and to sue for damage to the property. In a building with three or more households, the tenant must not wilfully or wantonly damage the property or let guests do so. An eviction complaint before a magisterial district judge can claim damages for injury to the property along with rent. No Pennsylvania statute lets a tenant end the lease or stop paying rent because of a fire or other casualty, so a tenant who caused the damage has no statutory casualty right to use; the library's optional casualty clause covers only damage the tenant did not cause. Two statutory rent remedies have no tenant-fault exception in their text: in cities covered by the Rent Withholding Act, rent is suspended and paid into escrow while the city or county certifies the home unfit for human habitation, and a tenant who pays your unpaid utility bill to keep service on may deduct it from rent. Whether rent continues during repairs and whether you can recover lost rent after the lease ends come from court decisions and the lease; the optional Damage Caused by Tenant clause covers both.

title: Waiving Habitability in Pennsylvania
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lists a landlord's repair duties or says whether a lease can waive them. The duty to keep a rental fit to live in comes from Pennsylvania court decisions (the implied warranty of habitability), and those decisions, not a statute, decide whether a tenant can give it up; this library did not read them and does not offer a habitability waiver. Two statutory rights tied to unfit housing apply whatever the lease says: in cities covered by the City Rent Withholding Act, once the city or county certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation, rent is paid into escrow instead of to you, and the tenant cannot be evicted while it is there; and a tenant who pays your unpaid utility bill to keep service on may deduct it from rent, a right no lease can waive. Any waiver of a tenant's rights that a lease does contain must be listed in the lease's Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to the Tenant
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute listing which repairs or services a landlord must provide, so there is no statutory duty for a lease to modify, and no statute requiring a separate document or a rent reduction when a tenant takes on a task. The lease may assign everyday tasks such as yard care, snow removal or replacing alarm batteries to the tenant, as several clauses in this library do. What a lease cannot reliably shift is the court-made duty to keep the home fit to live in (case law this library did not read), local housing-code duties placed on owners, and, in a building with three or more households, the statutory duty to use reasonable care to keep common stairways, passages and other facilities safe. Every task you shift should be named in the lease, and any waiver of a tenant's right must be listed in the Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: Tenant Rights a Pennsylvania Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general rule voiding every lease waiver, and no landlord-tenant code with one non-waiver section. Instead, particular statutes say their rights cannot be waived, and a lease term that tries is void: the security deposit cap and the deposit-return rules; a tenant's right in a building with three or more households to have guests, visitors and suppliers without a fee; the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act, including the right to deduct utility payments from rent; the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act; and exemptions from execution on a judgment. The City Rent Withholding Act applies whatever the lease says, and the protection-from-abuse hold on a victim's belongings applies even where the lease sets its own rules for property left behind. Some rights can be waived in the lease, such as the notice to quit (though federal law may still require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program), and the exemption from distress (a remedy this library does not use). Any waiver the lease does contain must be listed in its Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: Deposit Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Pennsylvania's security deposit rules cannot be given up in a lease. A lease term in which the tenant agrees to a larger deposit than the law allows, or gives up the written list of damages or the 30-day return rules, is void and unenforceable, and the statutory penalties still apply. The escrow, interest and transfer rules have no non-waiver sentence of their own; treat them as binding whatever the lease says. Write your deposit terms within the rules described in this library's deposit rows.

title: Smoke Drift and Smoking in Apartment Buildings
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking in enclosed public places and workplaces but not in a private residence, and it expressly lets a property owner ban smoking on its own property. No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to disclose that smoke may drift from other units, or lets a tenant waive a complaint about drifting smoke. Whether an enclosed common hallway, lobby or laundry room of an apartment building counts as a workplace where staff work there is not settled by the Act's text; the cautious course is to treat enclosed common areas where employees work as smoke-free. The Act's definition of smoking covers lighted tobacco and similar lighted products; Philadelphia has its own smoking ordinance, which this library does not cover. The library's smoking clause lets you set a smoking policy for the unit and the property.

title: Jury Waivers in Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: A Pennsylvania eviction is heard first by a magisterial district judge (in Philadelphia, the Municipal Court) without a jury. Either side may appeal to the court of common pleas for a new trial, and there a jury hears the case only if a party demands one in writing on time; otherwise the right is waived. The state constitution keeps the right to a jury trial inviolate, and the statute says a jury may be waived in the manner set by the court rules, which provide for waiver by not demanding one. No statute addresses a jury waiver signed in advance in a lease, and whether Pennsylvania courts enforce one in a residential lease is a question of case law this library did not read. The library does not offer a jury-waiver clause for Pennsylvania. If you add your own, it must be listed as a waiver in the lease's Statement of Consumer Restrictions; get legal advice first.

title: Clauses Excusing the Landlord from Liability
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bans, or expressly allows, a residential lease term excusing the landlord from liability for injury or property damage. Whether such a clause is enforced is decided by Pennsylvania court decisions, which this library did not read. Two statutes bear on it: a lease clause in which the tenant gives up a right must be listed in the lease's Statement of Consumer Restrictions, and a landlord is by statute not liable for injuries caused by an assistance or service animal it allows as a reasonable accommodation. The library does not offer a general liability waiver for Pennsylvania. Its parking, storage and renters-insurance clauses state who bears particular risks without a broad waiver.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute that lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term in a residential lease. The Commercial Code's unconscionability sections cover sales of goods and leases of goods, not leases of homes, and the arbitration statutes let a court refuse an unconscionable arbitration award. Whether a residential lease term is unconscionable is left to Pennsylvania court decisions, which this library did not read. Separately, a debt collection practice that is unfair or unconscionable, such as collecting a fee the lease does not authorize, violates the Fair Credit Extension Uniformity Act.

title: Attorney's Fees in Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires, bans or caps a lease clause shifting attorney's fees, and none makes such a clause reciprocal. A fee-shifting clause is enforced as a contract term, and how courts apply it is case law this library did not read; the Judicial Code's list of cases in which a court awards counsel fees does not include leases. The library's Default by Tenant clause lets the prevailing party recover reasonable attorney's fees to the extent the law permits. Several statutes give tenants their own right to fees against a landlord, including for unlawful disposal of a tenant's belongings, retaliation for using utility-service rights, and unfair or deceptive practices. Because a debt collection fee must be expressly authorized by the lease, state any fee you mean to collect in the lease itself.

title: Collection Fees for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Fair Credit Extension Uniformity Act covers a landlord collecting its own unpaid rent and other lease debts from an individual tenant, and its collection agencies and attorneys. Under it, a creditor may not collect any interest, fee, charge or expense on top of the debt unless the lease expressly authorizes it or the law permits it, and unfair, deceptive or harassing collection is a violation of the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law. No Pennsylvania statute caps a lease collection fee. If you want to recover collection-agency charges, say so in the lease (the optional Collection Costs clause does) and charge only what the agency actually charges you; a flat fee that is out of proportion to your actual cost may be refused by a court as a penalty.

title: Charging for Notices and Eviction Filings
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute authorizes or bans a lease charge for preparing or serving a notice to quit or a notice of default. A landlord who wins a possession case before a magisterial district judge is awarded court costs with the judgment, and the library's Default by Tenant clause covers reasonable costs and expenses the law allows. Because any fee collected on a lease debt must be expressly authorized by the lease, a separate notice fee would need its own lease term, and a flat fee out of proportion to your actual cost may be refused by a court as a penalty (case law this library did not read). The library offers no separate notice-service fee for Pennsylvania.

title: No Statute on Eviction Penalty Clauses
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bans a lease clause charging the tenant a fee or penalty if you file for eviction, and none authorizes one. Court costs are awarded with a possession judgment, attorney's fees only as the lease and the law allow, and any other fee, once it is part of a past-due debt, only if the lease expressly authorizes it. A fixed eviction charge that is out of proportion to your actual cost may be refused by a court as a penalty; that is case law, which this library did not read. The library does not offer an eviction-fee clause for Pennsylvania.

title: Liquidated Damages in Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs a residential lease clause that fixes damages in advance, such as a holdover charge or an early-termination fee. The Commercial Code's liquidated-damages rules cover sales and leases of goods, not leases of homes. Whether a fixed amount is enforceable as a reasonable estimate of loss or void as a penalty is decided by Pennsylvania court decisions, which this library did not read. The library's optional holdover charge and early-termination fee are written as reasonable estimates of a loss that is hard to measure, and a court can still review them.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice or Breach
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether accepting rent after you give a notice to quit, or after you learn the tenant broke the lease, waives the notice or the breach. That question is decided by court decisions, which this library did not read, and the answer can turn on the facts. The cautious course is to refuse or return any payment for a period after the notice, or to accept it only with a written statement that you accept it without waiving the notice or the breach, and to keep the lease's non-waiver clause (the optional No Waiver by Accepting Rent clause). In a case for unpaid rent only, a tenant may still stop removal by paying the rent in arrears and costs to the officer before the order for possession is carried out, whatever the lease says. For drug-related evictions, the statute says that not removing a tenant is not a waiver of your rights for later violations.

title: Lease Terms Pennsylvania Law Prohibits
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no single list of banned lease terms and no statute penalizing a landlord for knowingly using one. Specific statutes make particular terms void or limit them: a deposit above the statutory cap or any waiver of the deposit rules; a waiver of, or fee for, a tenant's right to have guests, visitors and suppliers in a building with three or more households; a waiver of utility-service tenant rights; a waiver of exemptions from execution; a waiver of Plain Language Consumer Contract Act rights; and terms overriding the City Rent Withholding Act. From December 21, 2026, a lease must say whether parking is provided and at what fee, and a parking fee may not be changed or added during the lease except as the statute allows; and an application fee must be reasonably related to actual administrative expenses. A confessed judgment for possession is not available on a residential lease signed by an individual. Every waiver of a tenant's rights in the lease must be listed in its Statement of Consumer Restrictions. Other limits, such as the penalty rule for fixed damages and the enforceability of liability waivers, come from case law this library did not read.

title: No Homestead Exemption, and Exemptions Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no homestead exemption protecting a debtor's home from creditors, so there is nothing of that kind for a lease to waive. The statutory exemptions from execution on a money judgment, such as $300 of property and certain specific items, cannot be waived in a lease or any other contract, before or after judgment. The 1951 Act's separate exemption from distress can be waived in writing, but the library does not use or offer distress. The library offers no exemption waiver for Pennsylvania.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Terms in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute on what happens to a residential lease when the home is damaged or destroyed by fire or another casualty, and no statute requiring a landlord to re-rent after a tenant leaves early. There is therefore no statutory casualty or mitigation right for a lease to waive; both are left to the lease and to court decisions, which this library did not read. The optional Casualty clause lets either side end the lease after a casualty the tenant did not cause, and the Default by Tenant clause promises reasonable efforts to re-rent where the law requires it. Rent paid into escrow under the City Rent Withholding Act, which applies whatever the lease says, is separate.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: Pennsylvania's arbitration statute makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, and nothing in it excludes residential leases. Possession cases and smaller money claims under the 1951 Act are heard by magisterial district judges, and some counties send appeals to court-run compulsory arbitration, which is a different thing from an arbitration clause. The library still does not offer its arbitration clause for Pennsylvania. The risk is the Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, which gives a tenant treble damages and attorney's fees for deceptive conduct: whether including an unenforceable term in a residential lease is deceptive conduct under that law is decided only by case law this library did not read, and the library does not offer a clause whose risk rests on that question. If you want arbitration, get legal advice, and list the jury-trial waiver it contains in the lease's Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: Consumer Protection Laws and Pennsylvania Leases
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law bans unfair and deceptive practices in trade and commerce, which it defines to include dealing in real property, and lets a person who leases goods or services for household purposes sue for actual damages or $100, up to three times actual damages, and attorney's fees. Whether and how it applies to a residential lease is decided by Pennsylvania court decisions, which this library did not read; treat it as applying. One statute removes the doubt for collection: the Fair Credit Extension Uniformity Act covers a landlord collecting rent or other lease debts from an individual, and its violations are violations of the consumer protection law. The Plain Language Consumer Contract Act separately requires a readable lease and a Statement of Consumer Restrictions. The consumer protection law's list of unfair practices does not name leaving blanks in a lease or failing to give the tenant a copy at signing.

title: No Penalty for Knowingly Using a Prohibited Term
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute that penalizes a landlord for knowingly putting a prohibited term in a lease. A void term is simply unenforceable. Penalties attach to conduct instead: double the wrongly withheld deposit, treble damages for disposing of a tenant's belongings unlawfully, damages for retaliation over utility-service rights, statutory damages for a lease that fails the plain-language test, and the consumer protection law's remedies for deceptive practices, which may reach a misleading lease term (case law, not read).

title: Pre-Set Deduction Schedules
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets a lease pre-set charges, such as a fixed cleaning or painting fee, to be taken from the security deposit, and none requires a notice before you use one. The deposit statute lets you keep only the actual amount of damage the tenant caused, plus unpaid rent or amounts owed for another breach, listed in writing within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept surrender, and you carry the burden of proving actual damage. A schedule of typical costs in the lease can tell the tenant what to expect, but each deduction must still be the actual, documented cost of damage the tenant caused. The library offers no pre-set deduction schedule for Pennsylvania.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund the tenant never claims, such as an uncashed refund check, does not become your property. Under Pennsylvania's unclaimed property law, property held or owing in the ordinary course of business that the holder has admitted in writing and that has been adjudicated to be due, and that stays unclaimed for more than three years without the owner showing an interest, is presumed abandoned. Whether an uncashed deposit refund meets that test is not settled by the text; the cautious course is to treat it as reportable. If the owner's address in your records is not known to be wrong and the amount is $50 or more, you must mail the owner a notice 60 to 120 days before the report is due, then report and pay the money to the State Treasurer. A holder who fails without proper cause to report or pay owes interest at 12% a year, among other remedies. No Pennsylvania statute lets a lease make an unclaimed refund the landlord's property; do not write one in. A tenant who leaves no forwarding address in writing relieves you of liability under the deposit-return section, but that subsection does not say the money becomes yours; handle it as unclaimed property as described above.

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives a tenant the right to pay the security deposit in installments, or requires you to offer that. You may agree to installments in the lease. Whatever the payment schedule, the total may not exceed two months' rent in the first year of the lease or one month's rent in later years or on renewal.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit Cap
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether last month's rent collected in advance counts toward the security-deposit cap, or limits how you may apply prepaid rent. The cap reaches sums deposited for damage to the premises or default in rent, which a prepaid last month's rent may be read to secure. The cautious course is to count any prepaid last month's rent toward the cap (two months' rent in the first year, one month's rent after that), apply it only to the last month's rent, and return it with any interest if the tenancy ends before that month. A servicemember who ends a lease under Pennsylvania's military early-termination law is owed a refund of rent paid in advance for the period after termination within 30 days.

title: When the Deposit Clock Starts
bodyText: Your 30 days to give the tenant a written list of damage, with the refund, start when the lease ends or when you accept the tenant's surrender of the property, whichever comes first. No statute requires you to give a notice when the tenant surrenders, or defines surrender. A tenant who does not give you a new address in writing when the lease ends or you accept surrender relieves you of liability under the deposit-return section, so ask in the lease for a forwarding address at move-out and keep a dated record of when you received the keys.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: The statute requires a deposit over $100 to be held in an escrow account at a regulated bank or savings institution (or covered by a guarantee bond instead), with written notice to the tenant of the bank and amount, and it says these provisions apply only after the second anniversary of the deposit. Read literally, the escrow, notice and interest duties begin at the second anniversary; the cautious course, which this library recommends, is to escrow every deposit over $100 from the start, with the bank notice, and to move it to an interest-bearing account by the second anniversary. You may keep interest equal to 1% a year of the deposit as your only administrative and custodial charge, and the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant and must be paid to the tenant every year on the anniversary of the start of the lease. Unpaid interest is returned with the deposit at the end of the tenancy.

title: Deposits When Rented Property Is Sold
bodyText: A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's duties and rights toward the tenant, including the deposit rules. No Pennsylvania statute says how deposits must be transferred at a sale, requires a notice to tenants of the transfer, or releases the seller once deposits are handed over. The cautious course: in the sale contract, transfer each tenant's deposit with its accrued interest to the buyer; the buyer then deposits the funds in its own escrow account and gives each tenant the written notice of the institution's name and address and the amount that the escrow rule requires whenever funds are deposited. A seller who keeps the deposits should expect the tenant to look to both seller and buyer.

title: Penalties for Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText: If you do not give the tenant a written list of damage within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept surrender, you lose all rights to keep any part of the deposit or its interest, and the right to sue the tenant for damage to the property. If you do not pay the balance within those 30 days, you can be liable for double the amount by which the deposit, with unpaid interest, exceeds the actual damage the tenant caused. You must prove the damage. The statute sets no separate money penalty for taking a deposit over the cap, or for missing the escrow or bank-notice rules, but any waiver of the deposit rules is void and over-cap sums must be returned. A tenant who gives no new address in writing at the end relieves you of liability under the return section.

title: No Rule on Posting Deposit Standards
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord, however many units it has, to post or give tenants the standards it uses to set deposit amounts. The cap still applies to every tenant, and fair housing law applies to how you set deposits.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs nonrefundable fees or requires a particular notice for one. The deposit cap reaches any sum required to be deposited for damage to the premises or default in rent, and the statute does not say whether calling such a sum a nonrefundable fee takes it outside the cap and the return rules. The cautious course: do not label money that secures damage or rent as nonrefundable; count it in the deposit. A true fee for a service, such as an application fee, is not a deposit, and from December 21, 2026 an application fee must be reasonably related to your actual administrative expenses. State every fee, its amount and that it is not refundable in the lease.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a separate notice, a separate signature or particular wording for a nonrefundable fee. State any nonrefundable amount in the lease itself, with its amount and purpose, as described in this library's row on nonrefundable fees.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs a holding deposit taken to reserve a unit before the lease is signed. If the holding deposit is applied to the security deposit once the lease is signed, treat it as part of the security deposit from the start: it counts toward the cap, and funds over $100 held to secure the rental agreement should go in escrow with the written bank notice (the statute's escrow section says it applies only after the second anniversary of the deposit, but escrowing from the start is the cautious course). Say in writing, before you take the money, whether it will be refunded if you or the applicant decide not to sign. A separate application fee is different: from December 21, 2026 it must be reasonably related to your actual administrative expenses.

title: Fees Instead of a Security Deposit
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute regulates a fee a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, such as a deposit-insurance or surety program. The 1951 Act lets a landlord post its own guarantee bond in place of holding deposits in escrow, but that is the landlord's bond, not a tenant fee. Whether a recurring fee that protects you against damage or unpaid rent is itself a sum deposited for those purposes, inside the cap and return rules, is not settled by the text. The library does not offer a deposit-alternative fee for Pennsylvania; if you use a program, state the fee and what it does and does not cover in the lease, and make clear the tenant still owes for damage the program does not pay.

title: No Fast-Track Deposit Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no special, faster or slower deposit procedure for abandonment, eviction, early termination or a tenant's death. The ordinary rule applies: a written list of damage and the refund within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept surrender, whichever comes first. A servicemember who ends a lease under the military early-termination law is owed a refund of rent paid in advance within 30 days.

title: Fees That Must Be in the Lease
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general rule listing which fees a lease must state, and no total-monthly-payment rule. Two rules come close. First, from December 21, 2026, the lease must say whether parking is provided and, if it is, whether there is a parking fee and its amount; if the lease is silent, parking is treated as not provided, and the parking fee may not be changed or added during the lease unless parking availability changes or a third-party parking provider changes its pass-through fee. Second, Pennsylvania's debt-collection law bars collecting a fee or charge that is part of a past-due lease debt from an individual tenant unless the lease expressly authorizes it or the law permits it. In practice, state every fee and charge, with its amount or how it is figured, in the lease.

title: Fee Transparency in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no all-in pricing rule for rentals: no statute requires advertised rent to include mandatory fees, a first-page fee list, or one labelled total of rent and fees. The rules that apply are general. The consumer protection law bars deceptive conduct, which can include misdescribing what a tenant will pay (case law this library did not read); a fee that becomes part of a past-due debt may be collected from an individual tenant only if the lease expressly authorizes it or the law permits it; and from December 21, 2026 the lease must state whether parking is provided and any parking fee. List every recurring and one-time fee in the lease.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute specifically bars a landlord from charging for a service or amenity it does not provide. Charging for something not provided can be a deceptive practice under the consumer protection law (case law this library did not read), and a landlord may collect a fee from an individual tenant only if the lease authorizes it. Two specific rules: a landlord may not charge a fee for a tenant's right to have guests and visitors in a building with three or more households, and from December 21, 2026 a lease silent about parking is treated as not providing it, so no parking fee can be added during the lease.

title: No Statutory Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Pennsylvania sets no limit on late fees for residential rent and requires no grace period. The lease controls the amount. A late fee out of proportion to your actual loss may be refused by a court as a penalty, and that is case law this library did not read. The library's Late Fee clause lets you set the amount and grace period.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Rent
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute addresses pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent. A refundable pet deposit is money held against damage, so count it in the security deposit and its cap, and hold and return it under the deposit rules, as the library's Pet Policy clause does. Monthly pet rent and any one-time pet fee must be stated in the lease. Pennsylvania's assistance-animal law sets documentation rules but says nothing about fees. Federal fair housing law governs fees for an assistance or service animal (not read in this pass); do not charge a pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent for one.

title: Collecting Rent and the Duty to Maintain
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute, like the uniform act's, saying that the right to collect rent cannot be separated from the duty to maintain the property. A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's duties and rights, and the court-made warranty of habitability (case law this library did not read) runs with the tenancy. In cities covered by the City Rent Withholding Act, rent is paid into escrow instead of to you while the city or county certifies the dwelling unfit for human habitation.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute allowing a landlord to lock out a tenant for unpaid rent, even with notice or in the lease. Possession is recovered through the magisterial district judge, and only the officer executing an order for possession may remove a tenant. The library does not offer a lockout clause for Pennsylvania. Disposing of or taking control of property in an occupied unit without the tenant's express permission exposes you to treble damages, attorney fees and costs.

title: Utility Deposits
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs a utility deposit a landlord collects from a tenant. If you take money to secure utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease, treat it as part of the security deposit: count it toward the cap, hold it and return it under the deposit rules, and say in the lease what it secures. Deposits that a public utility collects from its own residential customers are governed by Public Utility Commission rules, which this library did not read; the statutory chapter on utility customer deposits expired at the end of 2024.

title: Passing Government Fees to the Tenant
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a state rental license, registration or inspection fee, or says whether a landlord may pass a government fee on to the tenant. Many municipalities, including Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, set their own rental license and inspection fees by ordinance, and some limit who pays; this library does not cover local ordinances. If you want the tenant to reimburse a government fee, the lease must say so expressly, with the amount or how it is figured. The library offers no reimbursement clause for Pennsylvania, because the lawfulness of passing on a fee depends on the local ordinance that sets it.

title: Passing Municipal Fines to the Tenant
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bans or allows passing a municipal fine to the tenant. A fine for a condition the tenant caused may be recoverable as damages if the lease makes avoiding that condition the tenant's duty (contract law; case law not read), and a fee or charge on top of rent, once part of a past-due debt, may be collected from an individual tenant only if the lease expressly authorizes it or the law permits it. State law does protect against one kind of fine: a municipality may not penalize a resident, tenant or landlord under an ordinance for calls to police or emergency services made by or for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, where the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it actually was, so do not pass on, or charge for, such a fine.

title: Charging for a Removed or Disabled Alarm
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. For carbon monoxide alarms in multifamily rentals, the statute makes the occupant responsible for replacing any alarm stolen, removed, missing or made inoperable during the occupancy, and you must replace any such alarm left unreplaced before a new occupancy. If a tenant's breach costs you a replacement, recover the actual, documented cost as damages; a fixed fee may be refused by a court as a penalty (case law this library did not read). The library offers no tampering fee for Pennsylvania.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets a landlord require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, or sets a condition, age or depreciation test for carpet or paint deductions. A deduction from the deposit is limited to the actual cost of damage the tenant caused, listed within 30 days, and you must prove it. Cleaning needed only because of ordinary use is hard to justify as damage; if you want a move-out cleaning standard, state it in the lease and deduct only the actual cost of meeting it where the tenant left the unit dirtier or more damaged than that standard.

title: Pennsylvania Money Limits for Residential Leases
bodyText: Pennsylvania sets few money limits on a residential lease. Security deposit: two months' rent in the first year, one month's rent in later years or on renewal, and no increase in the deposit with a rent increase after five years' possession. Deposit interest: after the second anniversary, you keep 1% a year and pay the rest to the tenant. Application fee: from December 21, 2026, reasonably related to your actual administrative expenses. Guests: no fee in a building with three or more households. Interest: where a document calls for interest without a rate, the legal rate is 6% a year, and a court may allow interest at the legal rate on unpaid rent. Returned checks: a $50 service charge figure exists only as criminal restitution after a bad-check conviction. There is no general statewide cap on rent, rent increases, late fees, pet fees or other fees. For rent increases, the narrow exception is a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, where the tenant's terms may not be altered during the year after the conversion notice and an eligible tenant 62 or older or disabled who stays on longer may face an increase of no more than the lesser of 5% or the statutory price-index change.

title: Late Fees and Housing Subsidies
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a late-fee rule for a tenant whose rent is partly paid by a housing subsidy. Charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share, never because the housing agency paid its share late, and follow the subsidy program's rules and your contract with the agency, which this library did not read.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: In a suit for unpaid rent, a Pennsylvania court may allow interest at the legal rate if it finds that fair in the case, even without a lease term. The legal rate, where a law or document calls for interest without naming a rate, is 6% a year, and a money judgment bears interest at the lawful rate. Pennsylvania's usury law caps interest at 6% a year for the loan or use of money of $50,000 or less unless a statute allows more; whether that cap reaches interest a lease sets on unpaid rent is not settled by its text. The cautious course is to set no lease interest rate above 6% a year on unpaid rent or charges.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs rent concessions such as a free month or a move-in credit. Put each concession in the lease, with its amount and the months it covers, so the rent actually owed is clear. If you want any part repaid if the tenant breaks the lease, say so in the lease; a fee or charge that becomes part of a past-due lease debt can be collected from an individual tenant only if the lease expressly authorizes it or the law permits it.

title: Confidentiality for Domestic Violence Victims
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to keep a tenant's domestic-violence status or documents confidential. Two state rules protect victims in housing matters. A domestic violence affidavit a tenant files in an eviction case is not a public record. And a victim certified in the state's Address Confidentiality Program gets a substitute address that state and local government agencies must accept; the program discloses the real address only in narrow cases, though the program's duties bind agencies and the Office of Victim Advocate, not private landlords. The cautious course is to keep any information a tenant gives you about abuse private, share it only as the law requires, and accept a program participant's substitute address for mail where you can.

title: No Special Deposit Rule for Domestic Violence
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute changing the security deposit rules when a tenant leaves because of domestic violence, because it has no domestic-violence lease-termination statute. The ordinary rule applies: a written list of damage and the refund within 30 days after the lease ends or you accept surrender.
