Where co-tenants remain, the lease has not ended for them, so the deposit stays until it does; a protection-from-abuse order that excludes one tenant does not by itself end the lease.

title: Eviction Protections for Domestic Violence Victims
bodyText: Pennsylvania gives a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence three protections in an eviction. First, the victim has 30 days, not the usual 10, to appeal a residential possession judgment to the court of common pleas, and the appeal stops the eviction if the victim pays in cash, into an escrow account with the prothonotary, any rent that comes due during the appeal within ten days after each due date (every tenant who appeals must also deposit the rent due as determined by the lower court). Second, within 30 days after the judgment the victim may file a domestic violence affidavit that holds off the order for possession for up to 30 days after judgment. Third, if you know of or are told about a protection-from-abuse order protecting the tenant or a member of the tenant's immediate family, you must not, for 30 days from the date of the notice, dispose of or take control of the belongings the tenant left after an order for possession was executed, and a lease cannot change that. No Pennsylvania statute bars evicting a tenant because of domestic violence against them, but a municipality may not, by ordinance, penalize a resident, tenant or landlord for a call to police or emergency services by or for a victim of abuse or crime or a person in an emergency, if the caller reasonably believed help was needed or it actually was.

title: No Domestic Violence Lock-Change Statute
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute giving a domestic-violence victim a right to have the locks changed, or requiring a landlord to change them. A protection-from-abuse order can grant the victim possession of the home and exclude the abuser, which the court and police enforce. If a victim asks for a lock change, the cautious course is to make it promptly, at the tenant's cost only if the lease says so, and to give keys only to the tenants and occupants the lease and any court order allow.

title: Where Pennsylvania Protection-From-Abuse Law Sits
bodyText: Pennsylvania's protection-from-abuse law is Chapter 61 of Title 23 of the Consolidated Statutes (the Domestic Relations Code), which gives the definitions, the relief a court may order, including possession of a shared home, and enforcement. The landlord-tenant statutes refer to a protection-from-abuse order by name, not by an old chapter or act number, so no cross-reference has gone stale. No row in this library cites the former, separately numbered Protection From Abuse Act.

title: What Proves Domestic Violence in Pennsylvania Housing Rules
bodyText: Each Pennsylvania protection that turns on domestic violence uses its own proof. The 30-day appeal and rent-escrow supersedeas: a protection-from-abuse order, or other suitable evidence the court directs. The eviction stay: a domestic violence affidavit on the court's form in which the tenant affirms being a victim. The 30-day hold on belongings after an eviction: your actual knowledge of, or being notified of, a protection-from-abuse order protecting the tenant or a family member. The Address Confidentiality Program: certification by the Office of Victim Advocate. None of these lists a police report, a third-party statement or a self-certification letter to the landlord, and Pennsylvania has no domestic-violence lease-termination statute with its own document list.

title: When Pennsylvania Law Lets a Tenant End a Lease Early
bodyText: Pennsylvania lets a tenant end a residential lease early by statute in three cases. A servicemember or National Guard technician with permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders over three months, an honorable discharge or release, or orders to government quarters may end it by written notice effective at least 30 days after you receive it, with final rent prorated. A National Guard or reserve member called to active duty for 30 or more consecutive days may end a lease signed before the call-up without cost or penalty, by written notice. And the executor or administrator of a sole tenant who dies during the lease may end it on 14 days' written notice, effective on the later of the last day of the second calendar month after the month of death or surrender of the unit with all belongings removed, without penalty for early termination. Federal law adds its own servicemember rights. Pennsylvania has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early for domestic violence, age or illness, or because the landlord misrepresented the property.

title: No Early Termination for Age, Illness or Disability
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute letting a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or personal care home, and no rule ending a month-to-month tenancy on a party's incapacity. A tenant in that position ends the lease as the lease allows (for example, the optional early-termination clause) or by agreement. A request to end a lease early as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is a fair housing question. If a sole tenant dies, the executor or administrator may end the lease on 14 days' written notice.

title: No Statute on Ending a Lease After a Disaster
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute letting either party end a residential lease after a flood, contamination, other environmental event or government order makes the home unusable. The lease decides. The library's optional Casualty clause lets either side end the lease after a fire or other casualty the tenant did not cause that makes the home unfit to live in, and in cities covered by the City Rent Withholding Act, rent is suspended and paid into escrow while the city or county certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets a landlord or tenant end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or a share of the property's value, and none limits a tenant's repair remedies by cost. Pennsylvania has no statutory repair-and-deduct remedy at all; the tenant's remedies for a landlord's failure to repair come from court decisions (the implied warranty of habitability, not read) and, in covered cities, the City Rent Withholding Act.

title: A Landlord's Remedies When a Lease Ends
bodyText: When a tenant fails to pay rent, breaks a lease condition, or holds over at the end of the term, a Pennsylvania landlord gives the notice to quit (unless the lease waives it) and files a possession complaint before the magisterial district judge (in Philadelphia, the Municipal Court). The judgment can award possession, rent, damages for unjust detention and damage to the property, with costs. The landlord may also sue for rent alone in an ordinary civil action, and a court may allow interest at the legal rate on rent due. A magisterial district judge hears money claims up to $12,000; larger claims go to the court of common pleas. Distress (seizing belongings for rent) is still in the statute but the library does not use it. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: A Tenant's Remedies When the Landlord Breaches
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute listing a residential tenant's remedies when the landlord fails to repair or otherwise breaks the lease: no statutory right to end the lease on notice, to repair and deduct, or to withhold rent. Those remedies come from court decisions on the implied warranty of habitability, which this library did not read. Statutory remedies that do exist: in covered cities, rent withholding into escrow once a dwelling is certified unfit; paying the landlord's unpaid utility bill to keep service on and deducting it from rent; and, in a building with three or more households, a claim for the landlord's failure to use reasonable care over common areas. A tenant may also sue for damages for breach of the lease.

title: Early Move-Outs and Re-Renting
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says what happens when a tenant leaves before the lease ends: none keeps the lease enforceable for the rest of the term, none requires you to re-rent, and none defines abandonment of the home itself. The statute addresses only belongings left behind, which may be treated as abandoned in listed situations, such as a tenant who has left without saying they will return, with rent more than 15 days late, after you post notice of the tenant's rights. Whether you must try to re-rent and how your loss is measured are court-made rules this library did not read. Cautious course: make reasonable, documented efforts to re-rent at a fair rent, credit rent from a new tenant against what the old tenant owes, and get any agreement to end the lease in writing. The library's Default by Tenant clause promises reasonable efforts to mitigate where the law requires it, and the optional early-termination clause gives a fixed-term tenant a paid way out.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure in Pennsylvania
bodyText: A Pennsylvania landlord may recover possession when the term ends, when the lease is forfeited for breach of its conditions, or when rent is not paid after demand, and also for certain illegal drug activity. The statute gives no cure period before a notice to quit and does not say which lease terms are material; that is for the lease and the courts. The lease may shorten or waive the notice to quit. In a case for unpaid rent only, the tenant may stop removal by paying the rent in arrears and costs to the officer before the order for possession is executed. The library's Default by Tenant clause gives written notice and a chance to cure, except where the law allows proceeding without one. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: Notice Before Evicting for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Before filing to evict for unpaid rent, a Pennsylvania landlord demands the rent and gives a written notice to quit of 10 days. There is no statutory wording for the notice and no state form. It may be handed to the tenant, left at the main building on the premises, or posted conspicuously on the property. The lease may shorten or waive it (the optional Waiver of Notice to Quit clause), but a federal 30-day notice to vacate still applies to properties with federally backed mortgages or federal assistance. In a case for unpaid rent only, paying the rent in arrears and costs to the officer before the order for possession is executed stops the removal.

title: When Rent Cannot Be Demanded
bodyText: Pennsylvania suspends a landlord's right to collect rent in one situation: in cities of the first, second, second class A and third class, once the city or county certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation, the tenant's duty to pay and the landlord's right to collect rent are suspended until it is certified fit or the tenancy ends for another reason, and rent goes into escrow. Otherwise rent is due as the lease says. Before evicting for unpaid rent, you must demand it; the 10-day notice to quit follows the demand. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: Limits While a Notice to Vacate Runs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute generally limits what a landlord may do to the unit or the tenancy while a notice to quit is running, such as a ban on alterations that make the unit unlivable. The general rules still apply: no lockout or removal without a court order, no disposal of belongings in an occupied unit without the tenant's permission, and no shutting off landlord-held utilities without following the utility-service rules. In a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the tenancy's terms may not be changed during the conversion notice year.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring a tenant to give notice before leaving the home empty in cold weather, or setting a minimum heat a tenant must keep. The optional Cold Weather clause asks the tenant to keep the heat on and give notice of long absences in winter. Separately, Public Utility Commission rules on utility shutoffs may apply; this library did not read them.

title: Delays in Removal for Hardship
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute or court rule lets a court postpone a tenant's removal for general hardship such as illness, age, children, weather or inability to find housing. Two specific stays exist. When a member of the Pennsylvania National Guard or a reserve component is called to active duty, no eviction may be made from a home occupied by the member or the member's family without leave of court, and the court must stay the case for six months on request unless the military service has not materially affected the tenant's ability to pay; the court may adjust rent and later order the arrears paid. And a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence may file an affidavit that holds off removal for up to 30 days after judgment. The rules also build in waiting periods: the order for possession may be requested only after the 10th day following judgment, and the officer may remove the tenant on or after the 11th day after serving it. An appeal with rent paid into court stops removal while it is pending. Some counties offer eviction diversion or mediation by local rule, which this library does not cover.

title: Who Receives Eviction Papers
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute or court rule lets a lease name a person to receive eviction court papers for the tenant. The court serves the possession complaint itself, by mail and by the officer, under the court rules, and the notice to quit may be handed to the tenant, left at the main building on the premises or posted on the property. A tenant certified in the Address Confidentiality Program names the Office of Victim Advocate as agent to receive service of process. The library offers no service-designation clause for Pennsylvania.

title: Faster Eviction for Drug Activity
bodyText: Pennsylvania shortens the notice to quit to 10 days where a lease is ended because of illegal drug activity: a tenant's first conviction for illegal sale, manufacture or distribution, a second violation of the state drug act, or a seizure of illegal drugs on the leased premises, whether the home is a single-family dwelling, an apartment or a unit in a multiple dwelling. Not removing a tenant for one violation does not waive your rights for later ones. Separately, the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act lets a landlord, a tenant organization, a district attorney or, at a district attorney's request, the Attorney General bring an expedited civil action in the court of common pleas to remove people involved in drug-related criminal activity on or near leased residential premises, and the Drug Nuisance Law lets tenants, neighbors and others sue to abate a drug nuisance. No Pennsylvania statute fast-tracks eviction for other crimes. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute for an end-of-term possession bond or a bond with a confessed judgment for possession, and a confessed judgment for possession is not available on a residential lease signed by an individual. The bonds that exist are on appeal: a tenant who appeals may post a bond instead of cash for the rent deposit that stops the eviction. The library offers no possession bond for Pennsylvania.

title: Belongings Left After an Eviction
bodyText: Belongings left after an order for possession is executed may be treated as abandoned. Before removing or disposing of them, you must mail the tenant the statutory notice; the tenant has 10 days from the postmark to retrieve them or ask for storage of up to 30 days at a place you choose, at the tenant's cost, and you must use ordinary care with the property. If you know of or are told about a protection-from-abuse order protecting the tenant or a family member, hold the property for 30 days from the date of the notice. A written lease may set its own procedure for everything except that hold. A landlord who violates these rules owes treble damages, attorney fees and costs. The statute says nothing specific about pets or vehicles left behind, and gives no immunity for executing a writ.

title: Paying Rent into Court on Appeal
bodyText: In Pennsylvania, rent is paid into court when a tenant appeals a possession judgment. To stop the eviction while the appeal is pending, the tenant deposits the lesser of three months' rent or the rent in arrears (a domestic-violence victim deposits each month's rent as it comes due), then pays each month's rent into court; a low-income tenant may file an affidavit instead. You may ask the court to release the escrowed rent for the tenant's use of the home, and the tenant may ask for release to pay providers of services you are required to supply. Before the magisterial district judge, no rent deposit is required to defend, and a tenant may file a claim of its own at least five days before the hearing.

title: Removing Someone Who Was Never a Tenant
bodyText: Since 2024, Pennsylvania's landlord-tenant act does not apply to a person who is not and never has been a tenant, and its notice-to-quit section does not apply to recovering property from such a person. A tenant is a person who occupies with the owner's express or implied consent, including under an oral lease or where the owner or its agent accepted rent. Someone who is not a tenant, such as a squatter, is dealt with through criminal trespass (which covers entering or remaining after notice against trespass) or an ordinary civil action, not a landlord-tenant eviction. Pennsylvania has no special fast-track removal procedure for squatters. If the person may have a claim to be a tenant, treat them as one and use the eviction process.

title: Barring Someone from the Property
bodyText: A person who knowingly enters or stays somewhere after being told not to, by direct communication or by posted notice, commits defiant trespass under Pennsylvania's criminal law. A landlord may give that notice for areas it controls, such as common areas. But in a building with three or more households, the 1951 Act gives each tenant an unwaivable right to have guests and visitors for a reasonable time, so long as the tenant keeps the tenant's own obligations, which include not letting anyone willfully disturb other tenants or damage the property. The library does not offer a barred-person lease clause for Pennsylvania, because a clause requiring a tenant to keep out a person you name could conflict with that guest right. Bar a person from common areas by notice, and act against a tenant who lets a guest damage the property or disturb others.

title: Tenancies at Will in Pennsylvania
bodyText: A lease of more than three years that is not in writing and signed has only the effect of a tenancy at will, unless it has lasted more than a year and both sides have treated it as valid by claiming and paying rent, in which case it becomes a year-to-year tenancy. A tenancy with no fixed end, such as a tenancy at will, is ended by a 15-day notice to quit, or 10 days for unpaid rent, unless the lease waives or shortens the notice. Pennsylvania has no separate statute for tenancies by sufferance. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: No Special Rules for Seasonal Rentals
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute setting special rules for seasonal or vacation rentals of a home. A seasonal lease is an ordinary lease of a fixed term; if the tenant stays after it ends, the 15-day notice to quit applies unless the lease waives it. Short-term lodging regulation, taxes and zoning are set by other laws and local ordinances this library does not cover. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: No Automatic Renewal Statute
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute governing an automatic-renewal clause in a residential lease: no required type size, separate reminder notice or opt-in, and no limit on how early you may require a renewal decision. The optional Automatic Renewal clause renews the lease unless either side gives notice. Pennsylvania's health-club law regulates automatic renewals of those contracts only.

title: Ending a Lease for Owner Occupancy
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute giving or limiting a landlord's right to end a lease so that the owner or a family member can move in. At the end of a fixed term, or of a month-to-month period, you may end the tenancy without a reason by the notice to quit. During a fixed term you have that right only if the lease reserves it; the optional Owner Occupancy clause does, with at least 30 days' notice. A building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community has its own protections. Federal law may also require 30 days' notice to vacate for a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a covered federal housing program; see the CARES Act notice explainer.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute addresses renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, or sets a remedy for it. A landlord who does so breaks a lease with at least one of them, and the remedies are contract remedies decided by the courts (not read). If a unit can't be delivered on time, the lease's possession-delay clause governs.

title: Saving the Tenancy After a Forfeiture for Rent
bodyText: When a Pennsylvania landlord seeks possession only because rent is unpaid, the tenant can save the tenancy at any time before the order for possession is actually executed by paying the officer the rent actually in arrears and the costs; the order then has no effect. No statute gives a tenant relief from forfeiture for other breaches. The statute does not limit how often a tenant may use this right.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction
bodyText: In a Pennsylvania eviction for unpaid rent only, the tenant may stop removal by paying the officer the rent actually in arrears and the costs at any time before the order for possession is executed. You cannot refuse that payment to complete the eviction, the statute sets no limit on how many times a tenant may do this, and it does not require you to accept partial payment. A payment from a charity or agency made to the officer on the tenant's behalf is not addressed by the statute; the cautious course is to treat it as the tenant's payment. Accepting rent at other times is governed by the lease and court decisions.

title: Tenants When the Property Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no foreclosure statute written for residential tenants. After a sheriff's or other judicial sale, the purchaser may collect rent as landlord from the date of its deed; a tenant whose lease is older than the judgment or mortgage behind the sale keeps a right to possession that outranks the purchaser, and rent paid in advance is protected unless paid with notice of the proceedings or to defeat the purchaser. Federal law generally requires 90 days' notice to bona fide tenants after a foreclosure and lets a bona fide lease run to its end in many cases. A buyer of rented property takes on the seller's duties toward the tenant.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure to New Tenants
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a prospective tenant that the property is in foreclosure. Federal law protects bona fide tenants after a foreclosure sale. Telling a prospective tenant the truth if asked, and not misrepresenting the property's status, avoids a deceptive-practice claim under the consumer protection law.

title: Condemnation of Rented Property
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Eminent Domain Code treats tenants as condemnees with their own claims: the claims of all owners and tenants of condemned property are heard together, and the damages are fixed for the property as a whole and then apportioned among those entitled to them. The Code does not say whether a lease ends or rent is reduced when the property is taken; the lease decides. Many leases give the landlord any award for the leasehold, leaving the tenant only relocation and moving payments; whether such a clause controls the apportionment is a question of case law this library did not read, so the library offers no condemnation clause for Pennsylvania. If you use one, list the tenant's waiver of its share in the lease's Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: A Tenant's Bankruptcy
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says what happens to an eviction or a writ of possession when the tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law controls, including the automatic stay that can halt collection and eviction steps, and this library did not read it. The 1951 Act does not itself give rent a preference in a tenant's insolvency or bankruptcy; it leaves in place other laws on that subject (not read). If a tenant tells you of a bankruptcy filing, stop collection and get legal advice before taking the next step in the eviction.

title: No Defense for a Late Benefit Payment
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute or court rule gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement because a Social Security check, other benefit or housing-voucher payment arrived late. In a case for unpaid rent only, the tenant may still stop removal by paying the rent in arrears and costs before the order for possession is executed. Subsidy programs may have their own rules, which this library did not read.

title: Minors and Leases
bodyText: In Pennsylvania, anyone 18 or older can enter a binding contract, including a lease, and can sue and be sued. A person under 18 can raise minority as a defense to a contract, so a lease signed only by a minor may not be enforceable against them; have an adult sign as tenant or guarantor. No statute bars naming a minor as a defendant in an eviction, but court rules require a guardian for a minor party. The general definitions statute's use of 21 as the age of adulthood applies to reading other statutes, not to the right to contract.

title: Who May Appear for a Landlord Before a District Judge
bodyText: Before a magisterial district judge, an entity landlord may be represented by a lawyer, an officer, or an employee or authorized agent with personal knowledge of the case and written authorization from an officer; a partnership by a partner or an authorized employee or agent; and an individual landlord by themselves, a lawyer or an authorized representative with personal knowledge. The authorization is case by case, not a blanket appointment, and the rule does not let a non-lawyer run a business representing others. On appeal to the court of common pleas, the ordinary rules for representation apply.

title: Time Limits for Suing a Tenant
bodyText: A Pennsylvania suit on a written lease, for unpaid rent or damage, must generally be brought within four years, as must a suit on an unwritten agreement. A lease under seal can carry a 20-year limit, but only if the lease says so in the statutory words required for a contract under seal. Whether a partial payment restarts the period is a case-law question this library did not read. Other periods apply to particular claims, such as a tenant's action under the Plain Language Act, which must be brought within four years of signing.

title: No Rent Control in Pennsylvania
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statewide rent control or rent-increase cap, and no statute that expressly bars or allows local rent control. No Pennsylvania municipality is known to this library to have rent control, but local power is limited by statute: a home-rule municipality may not set duties or requirements on businesses except as a statewide or class statute expressly allows, and Philadelphia may not act contrary to statutes that apply across the state, though both may adopt building, safety, sanitation and health rules. Whether those limits bar a local rent-control, rental-registration or source-of-income ordinance is a question for the courts, which this library did not read. State law caps the security deposit and lets tenants in some cities pay rent into escrow while a home is certified unfit; it does not regulate the rent itself. Check local ordinances before relying on this row in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh or another home-rule municipality.

title: Landlord Registration and Rental Licenses
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statewide landlord registration or rental license. Many municipalities require one by ordinance (Philadelphia's rental license is the best known), and state law recognizes those licenses: when a municipality penalizes a tenant or landlord for calls for police or emergency help, a court may order the rental license or permit reinstated. No state statute makes registration a condition of filing an eviction; a local ordinance may (this library did not research ordinances). An entity landlord has two state registration duties that do affect court access: an out-of-state LLC, corporation or similar entity doing business in Pennsylvania may not bring a lawsuit, including an eviction, until it registers with the Department of State, and any entity that does business under a fictitious name may not bring a lawsuit until it registers the name. Owning real estate without more is not doing business for this purpose, but renting it out may be, so an out-of-state entity landlord should register before filing an eviction. Neither failure voids the lease, and the entity may still defend a suit.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires periodic inspection of rental housing, and none lets a lease give a housing inspector the right to enter a tenant's home. Municipalities may adopt property maintenance and housing codes and inspection programs by ordinance, and many do; an inspector who needs to enter an occupied home without the occupant's consent generally needs a warrant (a constitutional question this library did not research). The optional Cooperation with Inspections clause asks the tenant to cooperate and to tell you if they will not admit an inspector, without giving consent in advance.

title: No State Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statewide requirement that a landlord obtain a lead-safe or lead-free certificate or attach one to the lease. Federal law requires the lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978, which the library's Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause provides. Philadelphia requires lead-safe or lead-free certification for many rentals by ordinance; this library did not research it.

title: No State Rule on Health Department Rental Regulations
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give tenants a county or municipal health department's rental regulations, or to refer tenants to the health department. County and municipal health departments may adopt housing rules, and in cities covered by the City Rent Withholding Act a health or code agency's certification that a home is unfit suspends the duty to pay rent; when that happens and a tenant pays rent into escrow, the certifying agency sends the landlord a monthly statement of the escrowed funds.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute limits renting a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or sets a state lot-split or two-unit program. Zoning is local, under the Municipalities Planning Code, and a municipality's zoning ordinance may regulate uses, including rentals and short-term rentals, within limits the courts have drawn (not read).

title: No State Accessory Dwelling Unit Law
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute on accessory dwelling units: none requires municipalities to allow them, bars owner-occupancy conditions, or sets a minimum rental term. Whether and how an accessory unit may be built and rented is set by the local zoning ordinance. A lease of an accessory unit is an ordinary residential lease under the 1951 Act.

title: No Good-Cause Notice Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania state law has no good-cause or just-cause eviction rule and no notice a lease must give about one. A tenancy ends at the end of its term, or on a notice to quit for a periodic tenancy, without a stated reason, subject to the specific limits in state law (such as condominium-conversion protections and the bar on retaliation for utility payments). Philadelphia has its own good-cause rules for some leases by ordinance, which this library did not research.

title: No State Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no state-agency statement of tenant rights that a landlord must give or attach to a lease, and no rule barring suit until one is given. What a Pennsylvania lease must include is set by particular statutes, chiefly the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act's Statement of Consumer Restrictions (which the library's clause provides) and, from December 21, 2026, a statement of whether parking is provided. Some municipalities publish guides; Philadelphia requires certain notices by ordinance (not researched).

title: No State Rights and Responsibilities Guide
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give a state-published guide to tenant and landlord rights and responsibilities, at signing, renewal or any other time. The Plain Language Consumer Contract Act requires the lease itself to be clear and to list the restrictions on the tenant, which the library's Statement of Consumer Restrictions clause does.

title: Changing Lease Terms
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a notice period for changing the terms of a periodic tenancy. During a fixed term, the lease governs and a change needs the tenant's agreement unless the lease reserves it. For a month-to-month tenancy, a change is usually made by ending the tenancy with the notice to quit (15 days for a tenancy of one year or less or with no fixed end, unless the lease provides for a shorter notice or a waiver) and offering new terms. Two specific limits apply. From December 21, 2026, a landlord may not change or add a parking fee during a lease unless parking availability changes or a third-party parking provider changes its pass-through fee. And in a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the terms of a tenancy may not be changed without the tenant's express written consent during the year after the conversion notice (longer for eligible tenants 62 or older or disabled, though during that extension the landlord may raise the rent by up to the lesser of 5% or the statutory price-index change). A substantial change in the terms of tenancy within six months after a tenant uses Utility Service Tenants Rights Act rights to avoid a shutoff creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation.

title: Code Enforcement and Conservatorship
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute for appointing a receiver to repair an occupied, substandard rental building. Its conservatorship law covers buildings that have not been legally occupied for at least 12 months and meet other blight conditions; a court may then appoint a conservator to take possession and rehabilitate the building on a petition by the owner, a lienholder, a nearby resident or business owner, a qualifying nonprofit, or the municipality or school district. For occupied buildings, municipalities enforce their codes by citation and may sue an owner of property in serious violation of a code, including for penalties and the cost of repairs the municipality makes, and in equity. In covered cities a dwelling certified unfit triggers rent withholding into escrow.

title: Out-of-State Owners
bodyText: Pennsylvania does not require a nonresident owner to name an in-state agent in the lease or to hire an in-state manager, and no statute bars an eviction until one is named. Several state rules do reach out-of-state owners. Pennsylvania courts may exercise jurisdiction over anyone who owns or has an interest in real property here, and court papers may be served outside the state, including by certified mail in a case before a magisterial district judge. An out-of-state owner charged with a crime for code violations, after proper notice, may be extradited to face prosecution. An out-of-state entity must register with the Department of State before it can file a lawsuit here, including an eviction. And a business tenant that pays rent to a nonresident individual, estate or trust must withhold Pennsylvania income tax from the rent (optional when the lessor receives less than $5,000 a year); a tenant renting a home to live in is not paying in the course of a business, so this does not reach ordinary residential rent.

title: Police Calls, Crime-Free Leases and Reporting
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires a landlord to cooperate with police, or gives police a right to enter a rental unit. State law does protect calls for help: a municipality may not penalize a tenant, landlord or resident for calls to police or emergency services on behalf of a victim of abuse or a crime, or by a person in an emergency, and a court may undo such a penalty, including by reinstating a rental license. Landlords are not mandated reporters of child abuse by virtue of being landlords, but any person may report suspected child abuse to the Department of Human Services, the county agency or law enforcement. Illegal drug activity on the premises is a ground for a 10-day notice to quit.

title: Three Rules Pennsylvania Does Not Have
bodyText: Three common rules were checked across all of Pennsylvania's statutes, not only the landlord-tenant act. (1) Squatters: there is no fast-track removal outside the courts. Since 2024 the landlord-tenant act does not apply to someone who never was a tenant; such a person is dealt with through criminal trespass or an ordinary civil action. (2) Rent receipts: no statute requires a landlord to give a receipt for rent paid in cash; giving one is still good practice. (3) Landlord registration: no state statute makes registration a condition of an eviction judgment, though a local ordinance may, and an out-of-state entity or an entity using a fictitious name must register with the Department of State before it may file suit.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a residential lease to be recorded, and recording does not change any landlord-tenant right in the 1951 Act. A lease or a memorandum of lease may be recorded with the county recorder of deeds, and a tenant who mortgages a leasehold must record the mortgage with the lease or a memorandum. Whether an unrecorded lease binds a later buyer or lender turns on notice, including the tenant's possession, which is a question of case law this library did not read; the 1951 Act makes a buyer of rented property take on the seller's duties to the tenant.

title: Rules That Depend on Building or Portfolio Size
bodyText: No Pennsylvania landlord-tenant rule turns on how many units a landlord owns in all, and there is no general small-landlord exemption. Several rules turn on the building instead. The 1951 Act's tenant-rights article (guests, suppliers and common-area care) applies to a building with three or more households living in separate apartments; the drug-activity eviction grounds apply to single-family homes and apartments alike. The state fair housing law does not apply to a personal residence, meaning a building with living quarters for no more than two households that the owner or lessee lives in, and some of its exceptions cover a landlord-occupied rooming house or rooms in the landlord's own home; federal fair housing law has its own, separate exemptions. Deposit rules turn on time, not size: interest is owed only on a deposit held more than two years.

title: No General Tenant Right to Buy
bodyText: Pennsylvania gives residential tenants no general right to buy, or right of first refusal, when an owner sells a rental building, and requires no notice of a sale to tenants. The exception is a conversion to a condominium, cooperative or planned community: the developer must give each residential tenant a conversion notice at least a year before requiring them to leave, and for six months after the notice must offer to sell the tenant the unit they rent; for the next six months the developer may not offer it to anyone else on better terms.

title: No Exemption Notice for Sales
bodyText: Because Pennsylvania has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, there is no exemption notice or filing for an owner to give tenants or an agency when selling. The only tenant purchase right is in a conversion to a condominium, cooperative or planned community, and it has its own limits: it does not apply to a unit used only for nonresidential purposes before the conversion notice, or one whose boundaries will not substantially match the unit the tenant rents.

title: No Sunset on Tenant Protections
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute that protects tenants or governs renting carries a sunset or dated repeal clause: the 1951 Act, the City Rent Withholding Act, the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act and the conversion protections in the common-interest community laws have no expiry date. The 1951 Act's new parking and application-fee sections take effect on December 21, 2026 and have no end date.

title: Rent Increases During a Lease
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general statute on rent escalation clauses or mid-term rent increases. During a fixed term, the rent is what the lease says; an increase needs the tenant's agreement or a clause reserving it, such as the optional Mid-Term Rent Increase clause (30 days' written notice, with the tenant free to end the lease instead). No statute sets a general cap or a safe harbor tied to a written clause. The narrow exception is a building being converted to a condominium, cooperative or planned community: a tenant's terms may not be altered during the year after the conversion notice, and an eligible tenant 62 or older or disabled who stays on longer may face an increase of no more than the lesser of 5% or the statutory price-index change. Pennsylvania's only statutory retaliation presumption on rent is in the utility-service law (the Human Relations Act separately bars discriminating in any manner against a person who opposed a practice it forbids): an increase within six months after a tenant uses those rights creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation. From December 21, 2026, parking fees may not be changed during a lease except in limited cases.

title: Passing Tax Increases to Tenants
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets or bars a residential lease passing real estate tax or insurance increases to the tenant, or sets how the share must be stated or whether abatements must be refunded. A charge like this can be collected as part of a past-due debt only if the lease expressly provides for it or the law permits it, because Pennsylvania's debt-collection law bars a creditor from collecting from an individual, as part of a past-due debt, any amount (including a fee or charge) that the agreement creating the debt does not expressly authorize and the law does not permit. The optional Tax and Insurance Increases clause states the share, requires a copy of the bill and refunds the same share of any later reduction.

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no state tax on residential rent. The state hotel occupancy tax applies to rooms in a hotel, meaning a building where the public may obtain sleeping accommodations for pay, but not to a permanent resident, someone who has occupied or has the right to occupy the room for at least 30 consecutive days. Counties may levy their own hotel taxes under separate statutes (not read). A home rented for 30 days or more is outside the state hotel tax; a shorter rental may be inside it, and short-term rentals should be checked against state and local tax rules this library did not research.

title: No Statement of the Tax Share of Rent
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant what share of the rent goes to property taxes, on request or otherwise. Pennsylvania's Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program lets renters who are 65 or older (or whose spouse in the household is), widows or widowers 50 or older, and permanently disabled adults 18 or older claim a rebate from the Department of Revenue. For a renter, the law treats 20% of the rent actually paid to the landlord as property tax; the household income limit is $45,000 (adjusted each year for inflation), and the rebate is at most $1,000. The tenant proves the rent with a rent receipt or other proof of payment, and the law puts no duty on the landlord. A tenant of an owner whose property is exempt from real property taxes can't claim, and rent paid through a government subsidy doesn't count. Anyone who helps prepare or file a fraudulent claim commits a misdemeanor, so if a tenant asks you to confirm the rent paid, confirm it accurately.

title: No State Rule on Disclosing Code Orders
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a new tenant about outstanding inspection, code-violation or condemnation orders. A misrepresentation about the property's condition can still be a deceptive practice under the consumer protection law, so answer truthfully if asked, and do not rent a home that a code agency has condemned or ordered vacated. Some municipalities require disclosure by ordinance (not researched).

title: Rent When a Home Is Certified Unfit
bodyText: In cities of the first, second, second class A and third class, once the city or county certifies a dwelling unfit for human habitation, the tenant's duty to pay rent and the landlord's right to collect it are suspended until the dwelling is certified fit again or the tenancy ends for another reason. The tenant pays rent into an escrow account, which goes to the landlord if the dwelling is certified fit within six months, and the certifying agency sends the landlord a monthly statement of the escrowed funds. Outside those cities no statute bars collecting rent for a condemned home; a home that is unlawful to occupy should not be rented.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give a tenant a copy of, or disclose, a certificate of occupancy. The Construction Code Act requires a certificate of occupancy for new construction and covered alterations, and some municipalities require a use-and-occupancy or rental certificate before a unit is rented or re-rented; those ordinances were not researched.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give tenants, or attach to the lease, notice of a housing, health or sanitary code variance, exception or waiver. Pennsylvania has no statewide housing or sanitary code for existing rentals; those are municipal codes, which may have their own notice rules (not researched).

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code applies to building construction, alteration, repair and occupancy, but not to repairs or most alterations of existing residential buildings unless a local ordinance requires it, so it rarely governs an existing rental. The Construction Code Act adopted a fixed edition (the 1999 BOCA code and the 1998 one- and two-family code) and later editions only through a statutory review: a new edition's provisions take effect by regulation after review, and if an updated section is not adopted, the existing section stays in effect. The act was amended in May 2026 (Act 16 of 2026) to change that review process. Local property maintenance codes, which govern most existing rentals, adopt their own editions by ordinance.

title: A Tenant's Unpaid Water or Sewer Bill
bodyText: Unpaid municipal water and sewer charges can become a lien on the property under the Municipal Claim and Tax Lien Law. Pennsylvania limits an owner's liability for a tenant's bill in two kinds of systems. For water service through a separate meter and service line to a unit the owner does not live in, from a municipal authority or a third-class city, the owner is liable for the tenant's bill only if the authority or city notifies both owner and tenant within 30 days after the bill becomes overdue, and is not liable for service provided 90 or more days after the tenant's bill first became due (for an authority) or overdue (for a third-class city) unless a court order prevented a shutoff. For sewer service, the owner stays liable for the tenant's bill unless the authority or city fails to give the same 30-day notice. Give the water and sewer provider your correct mailing address so the notice reaches you, and require tenants to keep accounts current. Boroughs, townships and private utilities were not checked for a similar rule.

title: No Special District Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant that the property is in a special taxing, assessment, improvement or utility district. Pennsylvania municipalities may create neighborhood improvement districts, whose assessments fall on property owners, but the law imposes no disclosure to tenants; a lease that passes such an assessment to the tenant must say so expressly.

title: What Pennsylvania Habitability Law Does Not Contain
bodyText: This row lists what Pennsylvania statutes do not contain on habitability, so you know where the lease, local codes and court decisions do the work. No Pennsylvania statute: states a general duty to keep a rental fit to live in or an implied warranty of habitability (the warranty comes from court decisions); lists minimum standards for the inside of a rental unit, such as heat, hot water, locks or appliances; defines which defects are material; creates a presumption that a unit is uninhabitable; requires the lease to state that the unit is habitable; or gives a statewide repair-and-deduct right. What statutes do provide: rent withholding into escrow in covered cities once a dwelling is certified unfit; a duty of reasonable care for common areas in buildings with three or more households; the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act's protections when the landlord is the utility customer; and smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules. Most working standards are in municipal property maintenance and housing codes.

title: No Statute on Which Defects Are Material
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute defines which defects make a home uninhabitable or ties a tenant's remedy to how serious a defect is. Courts applying the implied warranty of habitability decide that case by case (decisions not read). Under the City Rent Withholding Act, the test is a city or county certification that the dwelling is unfit for human habitation, not a list of defects.

title: No Habitability Presumption
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute creates a presumption about habitability, such as that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable or that a landlord who fails to repair within a set time acted in bad faith. Pennsylvania's one statutory presumption in this area is about retaliation: a notice ending the tenancy, a rent increase or a substantial change in terms within six months after a tenant pays the utility or deducts those payments from rent under the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act to avoid a shutoff creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, but not for a notice ending the tenancy for nonpayment of rent that was not lawfully withheld.

title: No Required Habitability Statement
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires the lease to state that the landlord will deliver or keep the home fit to live in. The library's Landlord Maintenance clause states the landlord's repair duties as a contract term, and the implied warranty of habitability applies whatever the lease says.

title: No State Heating Standard
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a minimum indoor temperature for rentals, requires a landlord to supply heat, or limits shifting heat to the tenant. The lease and local housing codes decide. Where the landlord is the gas, electric or steam utility's customer for service to tenants, the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act requires advance notice to the tenants before a shutoff for the landlord's nonpayment and lets tenants pay to keep service on and deduct the payment from rent.

title: Fire Codes for Rentals
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statewide fire code for existing rental housing. The Uniform Construction Code under the Construction Code Act governs construction and alterations statewide; fire codes for existing buildings, and property maintenance codes, are adopted by municipalities, which may not set construction standards below the Uniform Construction Code. Philadelphia may adopt some later code provisions by ordinance. Ask the municipality which fire and property maintenance code edition it enforces.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit Duty
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to install fire sprinklers in an existing rental. For new one- and two-family homes, the Construction Code Act removes the model code's sprinkler requirement and instead requires the builder to offer the buyer the option of sprinklers at the buyer's expense, with cost and benefit information. Sprinkler requirements for new or altered apartment buildings come from the Uniform Construction Code.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure to Tenants
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant whether the home has fire sprinklers. The only sprinkler disclosure is a builder's offer to the buyer of a new one- or two-family home. This library found no state grant, loan or tax credit for sprinkler retrofits in the statutes searched.

title: No State Lock or Security Device Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or other security devices in rentals, or requires rekeying between tenants. Rekeying at turnover is still the cautious course. In buildings with three or more households, the landlord owes a duty of reasonable care for the safety of common areas it controls, and local codes may set lock rules.

title: No Smart Lock Statute
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute regulates smart locks, keyless or app-based entry systems in rentals, or lets a domestic-violence victim require a device provider to cut off another user's access. If you use smart locks, the lease's entry rules apply to their use, and the cautious course is to give each tenant their own credentials and remove a departing occupant's access promptly, consistent with any protection-from-abuse order.

title: No Key-Control or Staff Screening Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to keep a key-control policy or to run background checks on employees with access to units.

title: No Window Guard Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires window guards or regulates security bars on windows in rentals. Local building and fire codes may limit bars on windows needed for emergency escape.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to set a water heater to a maximum temperature at each new tenancy.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires steam radiator covers in rentals or a lease rider about them.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to supply a stove, range or refrigerator. The lease decides which appliances come with the home, and the library's Landlord Maintenance clause covers repair of the appliances that do. Local codes may require cooking facilities.

title: No Landlord Pool Safety Statute
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute puts pool barrier, fencing, lifeguard or safety-notice duties on a residential landlord. Pools used by the public may be regulated as public bathing places by Department of Health regulations, and municipalities often require pool fencing by ordinance; neither was researched here.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires periodic structural inspection of balconies, decks or other elevated elements of rental buildings. The duty of reasonable care for common areas in buildings with three or more households, and local codes, still apply.

title: Common Area Lighting
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets lighting standards for common areas or lets a lease charge a tenant for common-area lights. A landlord who keeps control of stairways, passages and other common areas of a building with three or more households owes a duty of reasonable care for their safe use, which includes adequate lighting as a practical matter. In a drug-nuisance case, a court may order the owner to increase lighting in common areas.

title: No Asbestos Notice to Tenants
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to notify tenants about asbestos in a rental. Asbestos removal is regulated as work (licensing and environmental rules not researched), and federal disclosure rules for asbestos do not apply to ordinary home rentals the way the lead-paint rule does.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires disclosure of defective or corrosive drywall in a rental.

title: No Contamination Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a residential lease to disclose that the property is contaminated or to incorporate a recorded environmental covenant. An environmental covenant recorded under Pennsylvania's environmental covenants law runs with the land, so its activity and use limits bind the property whether or not the lease mentions them; if a rental is subject to one, the cautious course is to tell the tenant about any limits that affect their use, such as no digging or no use of well water.

title: No State Lead Notices Beyond Federal
bodyText: Pennsylvania state law adds no lead notice, certificate or packet beyond the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978, which the library's Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause provides. Philadelphia has its own lead-safe certification rules by ordinance (not researched).

title: No Private Well Testing Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to test a private well or give test results to tenants. If a rental uses a private well, regular testing and sharing results with tenants is the cautious course.

title: Bed Bugs and Tenant Cooperation
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets landlord or tenant duties for bed bugs or other pests: no disclosure, treatment deadline or cooperation duty. The lease fills the gap; the optional Pest Cooperation clause has the tenant report suspected infestations, allow inspection and treatment under the lease's entry section and follow preparation instructions, and pay for treatment only when the tenant caused the infestation.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to notify tenants before pesticide application in a rental. Pesticide applicators are regulated under the Pesticide Control Act and its regulations, which were not researched here.

title: No Right to Install Air Conditioning
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives a tenant a right to install a window or portable air conditioner, or requires a lease that restricts them to say so. The lease decides; if it limits window units, say so plainly and allow safe alternatives where possible.

title: Shifting Maintenance to the Tenant
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether, or how, a lease may shift repair or maintenance duties to a residential tenant. Whether the implied warranty of habitability can be waived is decided by court decisions this library did not read (`edu-habitability-waiver-pa`), so a shift of duties that would leave the home unfit is risky; routine tasks the tenant agrees to do are a contract matter (decisions not read). The library's Tenant Maintenance clause covers ordinary upkeep, and the optional Tenant Repair Agreement clause covers specified tasks agreed in good faith.

title: A Landlord's Promises to Repair
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord's promise to clean, repair or improve a unit to be in writing or to carry a completion date. But a promise you make can bind you: failing to keep a written guarantee or warranty is a listed unfair practice under the consumer protection law, and misrepresenting the condition of a home is deceptive. Put any promised work in the lease or a signed addendum with a date, and do the work.

title: How Tenants Report Repairs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets how a tenant must give notice of a needed repair, or whether a lease may require written requests. The library's Landlord Maintenance clause asks for prompt written notice. Whether a landlord who knew of a defect can rely on the lack of written notice is a question for the courts (not read); the cautious course is to act on any notice you actually receive.

title: No Repair-Contact or Repairer Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to name a repair contact or approved repairer, sets a deadline for responding to repair requests, or gives tenants a statewide right to hire a repairer and deduct the cost from rent. Tenants' statutory payment rights are limited to paying a landlord's unpaid utility bill under the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act and rent withholding into escrow in covered cities.

title: Agreements for Tenants to Do Repairs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs agreements for a residential tenant to perform repairs or maintenance in exchange for a rent reduction or other consideration, and none requires a separate writing. The optional Tenant Repair Agreement clause lists specific tasks, states what the landlord gives in return, and keeps with the landlord any work needed to fix code violations affecting health and safety.

title: No Small-Landlord Escrow Exemption
bodyText: Pennsylvania's rent escrow remedy, under the City Rent Withholding Act, applies in covered cities to any dwelling certified unfit, with no exemption for small landlords and no exemption notice. Outside those cities there is no statutory escrow or repair remedy to opt out of.

title: No Alternate Housing Duty
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to provide or pay for alternate housing while a unit is repaired or after a fire or other casualty. The lease decides; the library's Casualty clause lets either side end the lease when a casualty the tenant did not cause makes the home unfit, with rent ending when the tenant leaves.

title: No Statute on Tenancies After a Disaster
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute ends a tenancy after a declared disaster, suspends rent while a home is inaccessible, or limits eviction during a disaster emergency. The Governor's emergency powers come from the Constitution and other law and could be used by order (not researched); otherwise the lease's casualty terms decide.

title: No Rule on Housing Disaster Evacuees
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets a tenant house people displaced by a disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, or bars a landlord from enforcing those limits after a disaster. In buildings with three or more households, a tenant already has an unwaivable right to have social guests for a reasonable period. A flexible response to a tenant housing evacuees is the cautious course.

title: No Government Shutdown Rent Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for government workers who miss pay because of a government shutdown or furlough. The lease's rent and late-fee terms apply; a payment plan for a tenant whose pay is interrupted is the cautious course.

title: Voucher Units and Repairs
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs how a housing-assistance payment is reduced or stopped when a voucher unit fails inspection. That is set by federal Housing Choice Voucher rules and the local housing authority's plan, which this library did not read. Separately, a court finding a drug-related nuisance may suspend government subsidies paid to the owner, such as tenant assistance payments, until the nuisance is abated.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs housing-authority inspections of voucher units or a tenant's refusal to allow one. Federal Housing Choice Voucher rules and the housing authority's plan control (not read). The lease's entry section governs your own entry.

title: Nuisance Actions Involving Rentals
bodyText: Several Pennsylvania laws let others act against a rental property used as a nuisance. Under the Drug Nuisance Law, a district attorney, the Attorney General at a district attorney's request, a county or municipal solicitor, a resident within 1,000 feet (including a tenant of the property), the owner, or a community organization may sue to abate a drug-related nuisance; the court may order repairs, better locks and lighting, rent paid into court for up to 90 days, a rent trustee, suspension of subsidies to the owner, or sealing the property. Keeping a public nuisance is a misdemeanor, and the court may order it abated. Municipalities may sue owners of property in serious code violation or regarded as a public nuisance. Illegal drug activity on the premises is also a ground to end a lease on a 10-day notice, and the Expedited Eviction of Drug Traffickers Act allows an expedited action. No statute requires a lease to summarize a criminal law.

title: No Chemical Warning Rule
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no law like California's Proposition 65 requiring warnings about chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm in rental housing.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to disclose nearby former military ordnance, a pending demolition permit, or shared utility meters. Where the landlord is the customer of a utility serving tenants, the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act gives tenants notice and payment rights before a shutoff.

title: No Military Installation Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a lease disclosure for property near a military installation or in an airport noise or accident zone, and none gives a tenant a termination right on that basis.

title: No Shoreline Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to disclose shoreline or beach access conditions in a lease.

title: No Stigmatized Property Statute
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute addresses whether a landlord must disclose that a death, crime or other stigmatizing event occurred at a rental, or protects a landlord who does not. Answer a prospective tenant's direct question truthfully, since a misrepresentation can be a deceptive practice. Refusing to rent because of a person's disability, which can include HIV status, is barred by the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and federal fair housing law.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure Duty
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell tenants about registered sexual offenders nearby or in the building. The Pennsylvania State Police publish information about certain registered offenders on a public website, and police notify neighbors about sexually violent predators. A lease may point tenants to the state website.

title: No Sex Offender Residency Rule for Rentals
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bars a registered sexual offender from renting a home near a school or other place, puts a duty on a landlord who rents to one, or makes it a crime to rent to two offenders who live together. The only occupancy limit is for group-based homes, which may not house more than five sexually violent predators at once, on penalty of a civil fine; that rule applies to group-based homes as defined in the Prisons and Parole Code, not to ordinary rentals, and the compiled section notes court decisions holding it unconstitutional as applied. Local residency ordinances may exist (not researched).

title: No Single-Family Rental Disclosure
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a special disclosure, with set type size or placement, when a single-family house is rented, or a statement of the home's permitted occupancy. Occupancy limits come from local codes and the lease, within fair housing limits.

title: Reselling Utilities to Tenants
bodyText: Pennsylvania caps what a landlord may charge a residential tenant when it buys utility service from a public utility and resells it: the bill may not exceed what the utility would charge its own residential customers for the same amount of service under its current residential rate. No Pennsylvania statute requires a submetering disclosure in the lease or sets a type size or format for one. The Public Utility Code excludes from the definition of a public utility a building owner or operator that both owns and manages the building's internal distribution system and supplies electric power to occupants; for gas, water and other services the statutes read do not say (Public Utility Commission regulations and decisions were not read). If you bill tenants for utilities, state the method in the lease and charge no more than the residential rate.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires building energy benchmarking or lets a lease clause authorize release of a tenant's energy usage data to the owner. Some cities have benchmarking ordinances (not researched). Utility rules on customer data were not read.

title: Meter and Conservation Charges
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to notify tenants of an energy-efficiency meter conservation charge or to deduct one from rent, and none regulates submetered water specifically. The general resale cap applies to water as to other utility service a landlord buys from a public utility and resells: the tenant's bill may not exceed the utility's residential rate for the same quantity.

title: Limits on Rebilling Utilities
bodyText: When a landlord buys service from a public utility and resells it to a residential tenant, the tenant's bill may not exceed what the utility would bill its own residential customers for the same quantity under its current residential rate. No Pennsylvania statute bars passing master-metered utility costs to tenants through rent or a separate charge, and none sets a utility allowance for unsubsidized rentals. Any separate utility charge should be stated in the lease, because Pennsylvania's debt-collection law bars collecting, as part of a past-due debt, a fee the agreement does not expressly authorize unless the law permits it.

title: Splitting Utility Costs Among Tenants
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bars or regulates a lease term making a tenant pay a share of utilities that are not separately metered to the unit, such as ratio billing by floor area or occupants. Such a term is enforceable only as the lease states it, and any resale of metered service is capped at the utility's residential rate. State the method and the share clearly in the lease, as the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act expects.

title: Submetering and Separate Utility Billing
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no statute requiring a lease disclosure, set format or type size for submetered or separately billed utilities, no regulator-prescribed submetering disclosure, and no billing-fee or late-fee cap for utility charge-backs. Two statutory rules apply. When a landlord buys service from a public utility and resells it, the tenant's bill may not exceed the utility's residential rate for the same quantity of service. And any separate utility charge should be stated in the lease, because a fee the agreement does not expressly authorize, and the law does not permit, may not be collected as part of a past-due debt. No statute addresses evicting for unpaid utility charges; the cautious course is to bill utilities as a separate, itemized charge stated in the lease and never to shut off service as self-help.

title: No Required Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a utility disclosure form or attachment to a residential lease, such as average utility costs or which utilities the tenant pays. The library's Utilities clause states who pays for each service.

title: Being Told About a Tenant’s Shutoff
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets an owner authorize a utility to notify it of a tenant's pending disconnection, or lets a tenant-customer designate the landlord to be copied on shutoff notices. Public Utility Commission regulations may provide third-party notice options (not read). Where the landlord is the utility's customer, the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act runs the other way: the utility must notify the tenants before shutting off service for the landlord's nonpayment. For water and sewer from a municipal authority or third-class city, the provider must notify the owner within 30 days after a tenant's bill becomes overdue to preserve the owner's liability.

title: No Submetered Service Interruption Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets an interruption or shutoff procedure for electricity or other service a landlord submeters to tenants. A landlord may not shut off service to force payment or a move-out; self-help is not allowed, and the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act protects tenants when a landlord who is the utility's customer falls behind.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules
bodyText: Pennsylvania's statutory shutoff protections for rentals are in the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act, which applies when the landlord is the utility's customer for gas, electric, steam or water service to tenants in a residential building: except in an emergency or where life or property is in danger, the utility must give the landlord 37 days' written notice and the tenants at least 30 days' notice before a shutoff for the landlord's nonpayment, and tenants may pay to keep service on and deduct payments from rent; a tenant's rights under the act cannot be waived. The separate statutory chapter on responsible utility customer protection (Chapter 14 of the Public Utility Code) expired at the end of 2024. Public Utility Commission regulations on shutoffs may still apply; this library did not read them.

title: No Utility Transfer Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs transferring utilities into a tenant's name, or lets a landlord cut off landlord-name service the tenant did not transfer. The lease decides who must open accounts; a landlord who stays the customer of record is a landlord ratepayer under the Utility Service Tenants Rights Act and must not leave tenants without service, and no landlord may cut off service as self-help.

title: No EV Charger Removal Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs what happens to a tenant-installed electric-vehicle charger at the end of a tenancy. The lease's alterations clause decides; require written consent before installation and say whether the tenant must remove the charger and restore the wall at move-out.

title: No Tenant Right to Install an EV Charger
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives a tenant a right to install an electric-vehicle charger or requires a landlord to provide one, and none brings a landlord's resale of charging into a weights-and-measures regime. A landlord who sells electricity to tenants through a charger should consider the resale cap and utility rules (not read).

title: No Shared EV Charging Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute regulates electric-vehicle charging stations in shared parking areas of rental properties. Charging rules belong in the lease's parking terms; from December 21, 2026, any fee tied to parking must be stated in the lease and may not be added or changed during the lease except as the law allows.

title: No Tenant Solar Right
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in or balcony solar device, or voids lease restrictions on solar equipment. The lease's alterations clause decides.

title: Cable Television Access
bodyText: Pennsylvania's landlord-tenant act protects tenants' access to cable television in buildings with three or more households. A landlord may not charge different rent or other charges to tenants who subscribe to cable and those who do not. Once the landlord and a cable operator have agreed, or an arbitrator has ruled, under the act's negotiation process, a tenant may request service from the operator of the tenant's choice and the landlord may not prevent it or block the operator's access to install and service its facilities. The landlord may require reasonable compensation from the operator for a permanent taking of property, and the operator is liable for physical damage. Service already provided when the article took effect is protected while tenants keep requesting it. Federal rules on satellite dishes and antennas in areas a tenant exclusively uses also apply (not read).

title: Recycling at Rental Properties
bodyText: Pennsylvania's recycling law requires larger municipalities to run recycling programs, and lets the owner or landlord of multifamily rental housing with four or more units meet its duty by setting up a collection system at each property: suitable containers for collecting and sorting materials, easily accessible container locations, and written instructions to the occupants on using the system. A landlord who does so is not liable for occupants who fail to comply. Whether your municipality must, or does, require recycling depends on its population and ordinance (not researched).

title: Parking Must Be Stated in the Lease
bodyText: From December 21, 2026, every Pennsylvania residential lease must say whether parking is provided. If it is, the lease must say whether the tenant pays a fee for it and, if so, how much. A lease that is silent counts as saying no parking is provided. During the lease you may not change or add a parking fee unless parking availability changes or a third-party parking provider changes a pass-through fee. A tenant may complain to the magisterial district judge (in Philadelphia, the Municipal Court), and a landlord found in violation must pay the tenant's parking costs for the length of the lease. Pennsylvania does not require parking to be priced separately from rent; the library's Parking clause lets you include it in rent or charge it separately, as long as the lease says which.

title: Parking and Towing Rules
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires parking or towing rules to be delivered before signing, set a heading for them, or limit what vehicle information a landlord may ask for. Two rules apply. From December 21, 2026, the lease must say whether parking is provided and any fee, and a parking fee may not be changed or added during the lease except as the law allows.
