And towing from a private lot is governed by the Vehicle Code's rules for posted private parking areas, including limits on storage charges where no municipal rate applies. Put parking rules in the lease or an attached addendum so they are part of the agreement.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Human Relations Act requires a landlord to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices or services when needed to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a home, and to permit reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's expense. In a rental, the landlord may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted. No Pennsylvania statute requires a restoration deposit to be held in an interest-bearing account, and none requires the restoration condition to appear in the lease. The library's No Alterations clause preserves modifications the law entitles the tenant to make.

title: Refusing an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Refusing to rent to, or discriminating against, a person because of their use of a guide or support animal, or refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal, is unlawful discrimination under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, enforced by the Human Relations Commission and the courts. Pennsylvania's criminal penalty for denying access to a person with a service, guide or support dog applies to theatres, hotels, restaurants and other places of public accommodation, entertainment or amusement; it does not name rental housing.

title: Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal in Housing
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Assistance and Service Animal Integrity Act makes misrepresentation in housing a crime. Intentionally misrepresenting a disability or a disability-related need for an assistance or service animal in housing, or making materially false statements to obtain documentation for one, is a third-degree misdemeanor. Intentionally creating or providing a document falsely stating that an animal is an assistance or service animal for use in housing, or fitting an animal with a vest, harness, collar or sign that falsely indicates it is one, is a summary offense with a fine of up to $1,000. These offenses are prosecuted by the authorities; they do not change a landlord's duty to consider a genuine request.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to give tenants a fact sheet about pets and eviction. The 1951 Act's rules for belongings left after an eviction do not mention animals; animal welfare law applies to any animal left behind (not researched).

title: Caring for a Tenant’s Animals in an Emergency
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lets a landlord enter to care for or remove a tenant's animals when the tenant is hospitalized, detained or otherwise absent. The optional Animal Care clause has the tenant name a caregiver and lets the landlord admit that person, or call an animal control officer, police or a shelter, after trying to reach the tenant.

title: Questions You May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Human Relations Act separately bars landlords from asking about protected characteristics, not just from discriminating. In connection with leasing a home you may not make any inquiry, elicit any information, make or keep any record, or use any application form with questions or entries about race, color, familial status, age, religious creed, ancestry, sex, national origin, handicap or disability, or a known relationship with a person with a disability, or about the use of a guide or support animal. Ask only what you need to apply neutral criteria, and keep documentation of a disability-related request separate and confidential.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute bars or requires asking about an applicant's immigration status, makes it unlawful to rent to someone unlawfully present, or gives immigrant tenants special protections. National-origin and ancestry discrimination is barred by the Human Relations Act, so a citizenship or status question used to screen out people of a particular origin is risky. Ask for the same identity and income documents from every applicant.

title: Children and Occupancy
bodyText: Familial status is a protected class under the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act: a landlord may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or advertise a preference because a household includes children, a pregnant person or someone getting custody. A landlord also may not evict before the end of the lease because of pregnancy or the birth of a child. No Pennsylvania statute requires the lease to address occupancy by children. Occupancy limits must be reasonable and applied equally; local codes may set them.

title: Screening Applicants
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no general tenant-screening statute: no rule on when criminal history may be checked, no look-back period, no minimum-income limit and no negligence shield for renting to someone with a record. One rule applies directly. Criminal history records that have been expunged or given limited access (including under the Clean Slate law) may not be used by any individual for housing purposes, except where federal law requires it, and an applicant asked about them may answer as if the offense did not occur. Screening must also follow the Human Relations Act's inquiry ban and the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (not read). Apply written criteria the same way to every applicant.

title: No Apartment Staff Screening Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires background checks on apartment employees. Expunged and limited-access records may not be used for employment purposes either, except where federal law requires it.

title: Protecting Tenant Information
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute specifically bars a landlord from disclosing tenant information. Pennsylvania's data-breach law applies to any entity that maintains computerized personal information, which can include a landlord holding applicants' Social Security, driver's license or bank account numbers: after a breach, the entity must notify affected residents without unreasonable delay. Limit what you collect, secure it, and share tenant information only as the law requires or the tenant consents. Victims in the Address Confidentiality Program may use a substitute address.

title: Tenant Records and Ledgers
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to keep a rent ledger, give one on request, or include one in a nonpayment notice. Pennsylvania's data-breach law reaches landlords that maintain computerized personal information such as applicants' Social Security or bank account numbers, and requires notice to affected residents after a breach; it does not prescribe a written security program for small businesses. A clear payment history helps in any eviction or deposit dispute.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires or regulates reporting rent payments to credit bureaus, requires landlords to offer positive rent reporting, or requires notice before reporting late rent. Federal credit-reporting law applies to anyone who furnishes information to a credit bureau (not read).

title: Tenant Associations
bodyText: A Pennsylvania landlord may not end or refuse to renew a residential lease because a tenant, or a member of the tenant's family, takes part in a tenants' organization or association. No statute gives tenants a right to meet in common areas or requires a landlord to recognize or bargain with a tenant group.

title: No Political Canvassing Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives candidates or canvassers a right to enter apartment buildings, or limits a landlord's rules on canvassing. Tenants in buildings with three or more households may invite visitors for a reasonable time, which includes people they choose to see.

title: No Religious Display Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives tenants a right to place religious or cultural items such as a mezuzah on a door frame. A rule that singles out religious items could violate the Human Relations Act's bar on religious discrimination; apply any door or display rule neutrally and consider accommodating small religious items.

title: No Flag or Sign Display Right
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives tenants a right to display flags or political signs at a rental, or limits a lease restriction on them. Federal law protects display of the U.S. flag only against condominium, cooperative and homeowners' association rules (not read). Any display rule should be neutral and stated in the lease or rules.

title: Firearms Rules in a Lease
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs firearm restrictions in a private residential lease, bars a landlord's rules on guns stored in vehicles in its parking areas, or makes a lease firearm ban unenforceable against a license holder. The Pennsylvania Constitution protects the right to bear arms against government action; whether it limits a private landlord's lease terms is a question for the courts (decisions not read). The library does not offer a Pennsylvania firearm clause; a landlord may set rules on safe storage and discharge as ordinary lease terms.

title: Marijuana in Rentals
bodyText: Pennsylvania allows only medical marijuana; recreational use is not legal. The Medical Marijuana Act gives patients no protection in housing, does not require landlords to allow use, and itself makes smoking medical marijuana unlawful, so a lease ban on smoking marijuana is consistent with state law. A landlord may also bar growing and possessing marijuana on the property; marijuana remains illegal under federal law, which matters for federally assisted housing. Reasonable accommodation requests involving medical marijuana are a fair housing question this library did not research.

title: Home-Based Businesses
bodyText: Pennsylvania's Municipalities Planning Code requires zoning ordinances to permit no-impact home-based businesses, such as an office with no customer traffic or employees beyond resident family members, in all residential zones as of right. That zoning permission does not override a deed restriction, covenant or agreement restricting the use of land, so a lease may still limit or bar a home business. Say in the lease what business use, if any, is allowed.

title: No Right to Run Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to let a tenant run a family child care home, or limits a lease that bars one. Child care homes are certified or registered by the Department of Human Services (rules not researched), and the lease's use clause decides whether one is allowed.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals. The optional Waterbeds clause requires the landlord's consent, a proper frame and liner, and water-damage insurance.

title: No Rule on Tenant Insurance Claims
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute governs how a tenant's renter's insurance claim interacts with the landlord's claim or the deposit, or bars a lease from requiring the tenant to claim against their own policy first.

title: Requiring Renter's Insurance
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute regulates a lease requirement that the tenant carry renter's insurance: none lets the tenant choose the carrier, limits force-placed coverage or admin fees, or requires a statement that the landlord's insurance does not cover the tenant's property. A requirement is a contract term. Any charge for coverage the landlord buys should be stated in the lease, because a fee the agreement does not expressly authorize, and the law does not permit, may not be collected as part of a past-due debt.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance. Some municipalities tie rental licenses to insurance (not researched).

title: No Student Housing Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets special rules for student housing or exempts it from tenant protections. Privately owned student rentals are ordinary residential leases; university-owned dormitories may fall outside the 1951 Act depending on the arrangement (not researched).

title: No Senior Housing Staff Card Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires work cards or special screening for staff of 55-and-older housing. Senior housing exemptions from familial-status rules come from federal law (not read).

title: Housing Provided to an Employee
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a signed disclosure when a landlord houses an employee, ends the occupancy automatically when the job ends, or says whether a caretaker is a tenant. Since 2024 the 1951 Act defines a tenant as someone who occupies with the owner's consent, which can include an employee; if an employee-occupant will not leave, use the eviction process. Put the housing terms, including what happens when employment ends, in writing.

title: No Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute gives landlords an incentive for renting to veterans or requires veteran-specific rent terms. Servicemembers have statutory early-termination and eviction-stay rights.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a residential lease to be translated, even when it was negotiated in another language. The Plain Language Consumer Contract Act requires the lease to be clear and understandable; if a tenant reads another language better, offering a translation is the cautious course, with the English text stated to control.

title: Foreign Ownership and Leasing
bodyText: Pennsylvania has old statutes on aliens holding land, which allow an alien who is not a subject of a power at war with the United States to purchase and hold up to 5,000 acres. They govern buying land, not renting a home, and no Pennsylvania statute bars foreign adversaries or nonresident aliens from leasing, requires a lease to a foreign person to say so, or puts any duty on a landlord to check a tenant's nationality. Refusing to rent because of national origin is barred by the Human Relations Act.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. State law already makes illegal drug activity on the premises, in a single-family home or an apartment, a ground to end the lease on a 10-day notice, and federal rules may require an addendum in assisted housing (not read).

title: Hunting on Rented Farmland
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute says whether a tenant of farmland has hunting or fishing rights, or whether the owner or the tenant may give permission to hunt. One Game Code rule bars hunting in unharvested buckwheat, corn, sorghum or soybean fields without the permission of the owner or person in charge. State in a farm lease who may hunt and who may give permission.

title: No Usufruct Rules
bodyText: Pennsylvania law does not use the civil-law usufruct. A person with a life estate or other limited interest may lease only what they hold; confirm the owner's authority before signing.

title: No Communal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no communal, tribal or native-owned land system requiring government approval of leases.

title: How Notices May Be Given
bodyText: Pennsylvania's notice to quit may be handed to the tenant, left at the main building on the premises, or posted conspicuously on the property; the statute does not mention text messages or email. Under the Electronic Transactions Act, parties who have agreed to deal electronically may give notices electronically, and a party may refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, a right the lease cannot waive. The cautious course is to give any statutory notice by a method the statute names, and to use email or text only as an additional copy the lease allows.

title: No Duty to Tell Tenants About Proceedings
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a residential landlord to tell tenants about a lawsuit, foreclosure, condemnation or code-enforcement proceeding affecting the property. Some proceedings reach tenants directly: a condominium or cooperative conversion requires notice to tenants, a condemnation lets tenants claim their own damages, and federal law requires notice to tenants after a foreclosure. Telling tenants promptly is the cautious course, and misleading them is a deceptive practice.

title: No Initialing or Bold-Type Rule
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease provisions or requires any lease term in bold, capitals or a minimum type size. The Plain Language Consumer Contract Act asks whether the lease as a whole is easy to read, considering type size, line length, margins and spacing and bold section captions; the Statement of Consumer Restrictions must be included. Initials on key clauses remain good evidence that they were brought to the tenant's attention.

title: Formalities for Long Leases
bodyText: A Pennsylvania lease for more than three years must be in writing and signed by the parties, or it has only the force of a tenancy at will (becoming year-to-year if it runs more than a year and both sides treat it as valid by paying and accepting rent). No statute requires a seal, notarization or a spouse's consent to lease, though if the property is owned by spouses or co-owners together, have every owner sign. A lease may state that it is under seal, which extends the time to sue on it to 20 years, only with the statutory sealed-contract statement.

title: No Rule on Month-to-Month Premiums
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute limits charging a month-to-month tenant more, or setting different terms, than a fixed-term tenant.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute sets a minimum type size for a residential lease. The Plain Language Consumer Contract Act considers whether type size, spacing and layout make the lease easy to read, and a lease that fails its tests exposes the landlord to the act's remedies. Use at least 10-point type and bold section headings as a practical floor.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Pennsylvania a lease of real property for up to three years may be made by oral or written agreement. A lease for more than three years must be in writing and signed by the parties or their authorized agents; otherwise it is only a tenancy at will, becoming year-to-year if it continues more than a year with rent paid and accepted. Recording is not required for validity. Put every residential lease in writing anyway: the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act's Statement of Consumer Restrictions and, from December 21, 2026, the parking statement must be in the lease.

title: Which Notices Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Pennsylvania requires writing for the notices that matter most: the landlord's notice to quit must be in writing; the itemized list of deposit deductions must be written and given within 30 days; an executor ending a deceased tenant's lease gives written notice; a servicemember ends a lease by written notice; and the post-eviction notice about belongings is written and mailed. The lease decides how other notices are given; the library's Notices clause requires writing.

title: No Statutory List of Facilities
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute lists facilities a landlord must supply or puts product-safety duties on a landlord for building equipment such as garage door openers, elevators or laundry machines. The lease should list every facility and shared amenity provided; elevators and similar equipment are regulated under other laws and local codes (not researched).

title: Illegal Use of the Premises
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute voids or annuls a residential lease automatically when the premises are used for an illegal purpose. Illegal drug activity on the premises, in a single-family home or an apartment, is a breach of the lease and a ground to end it on a 10-day notice, a drug-related nuisance can be abated by court order, and other illegal use can be a breach of the lease's use clause supporting a notice to quit.

title: A Tenant's Duties Under Pennsylvania Law
bodyText: In buildings with three or more households, the 1951 Act requires a tenant to comply with all obligations that municipal, county and state codes place on tenants, and in particular not to willfully or wantonly destroy, damage or remove any part of the unit or common facilities, or let anyone on the premises with permission do so, and not to let anyone willfully or wantonly disturb other tenants' and neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. No statute lists tenant duties for smaller buildings; the lease does, through the library's Tenant Maintenance and use clauses.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Pennsylvania has no truth-in-renting law requiring a state statement of rights or voiding lease terms that misstate the law. The consumer protection law covers much of the same ground: misrepresenting a tenant's rights or the property, or including terms the law makes void, can be a deceptive practice, and the Plain Language Consumer Contract Act requires a clear lease with a Statement of Consumer Restrictions.

title: Penalties Tied to the Deposit List
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a landlord to tell a tenant about a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving that notice out. The penalty Pennsylvania does impose is tied to the deposit: a landlord who does not give the written list of damages within 30 days after the lease ends or the unit is surrendered forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit for damages and to sue the tenant for damage to the premises, and a landlord who fails to return the balance within 30 days owes double the amount wrongfully withheld.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: Under Pennsylvania's Mechanics' Lien Law, a tenant who orders work is an owner of its leasehold, and a contractor's lien binds only the interest of the party named as owner when the contract was made. Consenting to a tenant's improvement does not expose the landlord's ownership to a lien unless the landlord signed a writing showing the work was in fact for the landlord's immediate use and benefit. The optional No Liens clause makes the tenant pay its contractors, have any lien released, and tell contractors it alone is responsible. Avoid signing anything stating that a tenant's work is for your benefit unless you mean to pay for it.

title: Renting a Condominium or Planned-Community Unit
bodyText: Pennsylvania's condominium and planned community acts let an association, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules, and charge for late assessments; the fines run against the unit owner. The acts set no cap on lease-approval fees, no association-held tenant deposit rule, no right for the association to collect rent from a tenant when the owner is delinquent, and no rule on when a rental restriction binds existing owners; the declaration, bylaws and case law decide those (not read). If your unit is in an association, attach its rules, make the lease subject to any required approval, and use the library's Association Compliance clause to pass fines caused by the tenant to the tenant.

title: No Association Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute requires a lease of a condominium or planned-community unit to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, or to include an owner's statement about the association law. Resale certificates and seller disclosures apply to sales, including a lease with an option to purchase (see Required Disclosures). Giving the tenant the association rules that apply to residents is the cautious course.

title: What a Pennsylvania Lease Must Contain
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute prescribes the full contents of a residential lease or requires the start and end dates on the first page. What the law does require in the lease: a Statement of Consumer Restrictions listing what the tenant could lose and any rights the tenant gives up (Plain Language Consumer Contract Act); from December 21, 2026, a statement of whether parking is provided and any parking fee; and, for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure. The library's required clauses cover each.

title: Required Disclosures, Including Lease-Options
bodyText: Pennsylvania's required lease disclosures are the Statement of Consumer Restrictions and, from December 21, 2026, the parking statement, plus the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing. No statute requires a just-cause or rent-law coverage notice, a state form as the first page, or a licensee status statement in the lease. A lease with an option to purchase is different: Pennsylvania's Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law applies to a transfer of one to four residential units by a lease with an option to purchase, so the owner must give the seller's property disclosure statement as the law requires for a sale.

title: Options to Purchase
bodyText: No Pennsylvania statute regulates an option to purchase signed with a residential lease, such as required contract terms or a cancellation statement. But a lease with an option to purchase one to four residential units is a residential real estate transfer under the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, so the seller's property disclosure duties apply. The library offers no lease-option clause; get legal advice before granting one.

title: Other Rules Pennsylvania Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some states for which Pennsylvania has no statute, each explained in its own row: no good-cause eviction rule; no general anti-retaliation law (only the utility-payment presumption and protection for tenants' association participation); no lockout or self-help eviction right; no statutory entry notice; no repair-and-deduct remedy; no rent control; no move-in inspection rule; no lease-copy, initialing or type-size rule; and no truth-in-renting law.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Pennsylvania follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (13 Pa.C.S. § 3311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (13 Pa.C.S. § 1308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Pennsylvania's landlord-tenant statute imposes no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: the Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951 (68 P.S. § 250.101 et seq.) does not use the words 'good faith' at all. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Pennsylvania's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
